title: TCL’s first NXTPAPER phone with AMOLED is also one of its most flagship-like, coming to US
snippet: After showing off a proof-of-concept back at CES 2026 earlier this year, TCL is officially making its first NXTPAPER phones with AMOLED displays – the TCL P80 series. more…
fullText:
After showing off a proof-of-concept back at CES 2026 earlier this year, TCL is officially making its first NXTPAPER phones with AMOLED displays – the TCL P80 series.

TCL’s NXTPAPER display tech is more than just a matte coating, but the one part that takes the whole thing down a notch has been the panel technology. While NXTPAPER displays typically look good, they lack the vibrance and brightness of the AMOLED (or OLED) panels used on most other modern smartphones. That’s finally changing, with the first new releases dropping this week.

TCL P80, P80 Pro, and P80 Ultra offer up a 1.5K NXTPAPER AMOLED display and some of the highest-end packages TCL has put together so far – though still not quite in flagship territory. All three phones are based on MediaTek chips, with Ultra and Pro using Dimensity 7400 Elite and the base model a Dimensity 7300 Elite. These are upper-mid-range chips that are still a whole lot more powerful than what TCL’s phones usually bring to the table. They’ve all got a 6.83-inch display.

The TCL P80 Ultra has two 50MP cameras on the back including a telephoto lens, up to 512GB of storage, 8GB of RAM, a 6,800 mAh battery, and IP68 dust/water resistance.  TCL P80 Pro is virtually identical, but the second 50MP camera is now an 8MP ultrawide. The base TCL P80 also has a 50MP main camera and 8MP ultrawide, but has the aforementioned drop in chipset, as well as limiting itself to 256GB of storage at most, while still offering 8GB of RAM. It also drops down to a 6,000 mAh battery. 

	

These phones launch in Europe starting today at €349, €429, and €549, respectively.

TCL says these phones will come to the US eventually, but there’s no exact word on when. TCL is supporting the Ultra with 7 years of OS and security updates, while the Pro and base models drop to 3 years of OS updates, but stick with 7 years of security updates.

title: Google Chrome starts two-week release cycle with version 153
snippet: As previewed earlier this year, Google Chrome is now operating on a two-week release cycle. more…
fullText:
As previewed earlier this year, Google Chrome is now operating on a two-week release cycle.

Previously, Chrome received a major “milestone” update — like going from version 100 to 101 — every four weeks. Before 2021, Google had a six-week cycle.

The aim of releasing big updates every two weeks is to deliver “new features, performance improvements, and bug fixes faster.” Less is included with each update, but that will be paired with the increased frequency.

Meanwhile, Google says this “increased cadence is a win for the entire web.” Developers will be able to “ship modern web features with confidence, knowing that deployment windows are tighter, interoperability updates arrive quickly, and safety improvements reach users faster across platforms.” The fact that the “scope per release is smaller” will make “regression isolation faster.”

	

On the security front, Google says this change will “protect against fast-moving threats” given the rise of AI.

For enterprise customers, Chrome offers the “Extended Stable” channel that updates in eight-week increments: Chrome 156 followed by version 160. Google says most enterprise users should be on the two-week Stable option.

Chrome 153 is rolling out starting today for desktop, Android, and iOS. Meanwhile, version 154 will be available on September 22.

title: Google’s AI also cheats, but a little more honestly
snippet: Hey, happy Tuesday. How was your long weekend? I hope it involved a little Windows 98-style downtime, maybe some pickleball with Andre Agassi, a dive into the origins of the newly UN-endorsed Equal Earth map, and a few examples of GPT-6 Astra blowing some minds. As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe. more…
fullText:
Hey, happy Tuesday. How was your long weekend? I hope it involved a little Windows 98-style downtime, maybe some pickleball with Andre Agassi, a dive into the origins of the newly UN-endorsed Equal Earth map, and a few examples of GPT-6 Astra blowing some minds.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

In early September, Google DeepMind published a paper (via Import AI) that had a few parallels to the OpenAI-Hugging Face attack, though without the sandbox-escaping consequences. Instead, the company challenged 100 autonomous agents to solve 71 math problems. Though they could talk to one another and were allowed to share resources, they were explicitly warned not to cheat.

	

However, several minutes into the run, one of the agents found an exploit: “Over the following 27 minutes, the exploit spread virally through the swarm’s shared knowledge library, and the research collective unexpectedly ‘solved’ the remaining 34 problems.”

What’s really interesting about these findings is the percentage of agents complicit in the mischief: only 9% actively took advantage of the exploit; 5% were “converted” by the exploiters; 24% were considered “whistleblowers” and refused to cheat, attempting to contact the authorities instead; and 62% stayed unaware of the contagion and continued to operate as normal.

The paper ultimately argues that while some of the agents are prone to taking advantage of exploits, it’s largely a product of design and oversight more than inherent behavior. “Our findings show that the same infrastructure that allows the agents to coordinate and collaborate, if left unmanaged or poorly designed, also makes the system highly vulnerable to rapid pollution with specification gaming and reward hacks. Equipping agent collectives with the institutional infrastructure to translate emergent peer oversight into actionable self-governance offers a promising blueprint for scaling autonomous scientific discovery reliably.” 

In other words, they want to be good; they just need the right environment in which to do so. Sound familiar?

✉️ Inbox

A pile of MacBook Neo clones gives Googlebook all the more of an uphill battle. Ben’s Weekender essay dives into the miasma of what Google is jumping into with its Googlebook line.

Gemini Spark rolling out Google Photos control for automated editing, sharing, & more. I’m really curious about whether people will use this to batch-edit or better organize their libraries. I’m going to be testing it out.

Ugreen’s ‘HomeAgent’ is a local AI smart home ecosystem for its new line of cameras, more. This, along with Anker’s MindBase, is the beginning of what I think is a long road toward bringing local AI into the mainstream. Having a dedicated box with enough compute to control a smart home or NAS, and be a centralized hub for distributed private AI, is pretty compelling.

This Android phone has a detachable action camera, coming to the US for $999. I hate how much I love this idea.

Sony WH-1000XM4C launch for $299 alongside two more affordable headphones. In a world where everything is getting more expensive, it’s a pretty good idea to relaunch a 6-year-old product at half its original price. Still nowhere near a bargain, though.

🤝 Cc: Will Sattelberg

Welcome to a new project I’m calling Cc, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, 9to5Google’s superb podcast host and long-suffering Bills fan, Will Sattelberg.

Who are you?

Isn’t that the question we all ask ourselves in front of the mirror every morning? (I’m Will Sattelberg.)

What do you do for work?

I’m some combination of a writer and a podcaster. I guess I mostly make things online for people to enjoy, hopefully.

What do you do for fun?

Some combination of indoor kid hobbies (gaming, movies, cooking, D&D) and outdoor hobbies (running, long walks, traveling). We also have two cats in our house that we enjoy hanging out with, although only one of them is really playful in any sense of the word.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

In all honesty, not great — click on any random episode of The Sideload to hear my mental anguish on a near-weekly basis (Ed. Also listen to Pixelated, the other show he co-hosts.). I really fell in love with technology as an adolescent (I started listening to CNET’s Buzz Out Loud when I was 13) and getting to cover it professionally was sort of the end result of a dream I didn’t even realize I was chasing. But like lots of things that are in your life long enough, eventually your relationship with an interest begins to reshape itself.

Frankly, a lot of the elements of technology that first got me hooked on gadgets have been left in the rearview mirror by the most notable names in the industry — Google included — while the slow death of both traditional websites with front pages worth visiting and the feed-based social networks that originally killed them off has made it more difficult to really feel like you’re in the conversation to begin with. 

These days, the technology that makes me happiest tends to be single-purpose devices designed to accomplish a few things really well, rather than following through on the jack-of-all-trades, AI-will-fix-it routine. Mostly, I just hope brighter days are around the corner.

What are a few apps you can’t live without and why?

I’ll need to start by echoing David Imel on Pocket Casts. I haven’t used the app quite as long as him (mine says I’ve been listening since November 22nd, 2015), but my listening time is, no joke, just two days’ worth of playback away from hitting a full 365 days. Crazy stuff.

Letterboxd remains indispensable for movie fans, even if — like me — you mostly use it these days just to log whatever you’re watching to your diary. I have over a decade’s worth of movie-watching experiences logged on there with only a couple of gaps, and being able to look back at what I was watching 10 years ago is a genuinely cool feat. I just hope the app doesn’t sell.

Finally, this one’s actually fairly new to my app drawer, but I’ve been using Rise to get my sleep schedule back under control, and even after just a few weeks of use, I have been going to bed at a more regular (and reasonable) time, and I’m already noticing an overall difference in my energy levels.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Technically it started shipping to early adopters late last year, but the AYN Thor is by far my contender for favorite gadget of 2026. It’s an Android-powered emulation handheld designed to mirror Nintendo’s 3DS family, but with all sorts of modern touches. I’d love to tell you I’ve finally filled in my DS and 3DS gaps, but truth be told, I mostly use it to play all sorts of weird and wild Pokémon ROM hacks, like — most recently — the Creepypasta-inspired entry Pokémon: Ghost Grey.

What’s a recent TV show you loved?

My fiancée and I, frustrated as ever with the current slate of streaming shows, have mostly been diving into the archives to fill in some backlog gaps (most recently Sex and the City, which I enjoyed far more than I thought I would. Carrie Bradshaw deserves as much credit for the antihero trend as Tony Soprano and I’ll die on this hill), but I will shout out two fairly different shows as recommendations. 

First, Widow’s Bay really is as good as everyone is saying. Blew me away in pretty much every way it could, from the acting to the writing to the cinematography. A really fresh spin on “horror-comedy,” a genre I think can get old fast.

I’ll also shout out Taskmaster, which, full disclosure, my friend and former boss James Peckham recommended to me in 2023 at a cafe in Barcelona and I still dragged my feet for two additional years until Jason Mantzoukas showed up. Anyway, the entire 21-season (series, Jason) run is officially available on YouTube, and series 22 just started airing, so it’s a great time to check it out. If you have any love or fondness for classic Whose Line is it Anyway?, I think you’ll get a huge kick out of it.

What’s a recent movie you loved?

I’ll be honest, I’ve been slacking on my new release movies this year, but I’ll echo David’s shoutout of The Drama as a film I both liked more than I thought I would and one that has stayed with me longer than I anticipated. My favorite Zendaya performance so far, and it’s not even close.

What’s a recent game you loved?

As for games, “recent” gets complicated (I’ve been trying to clear out some of my backlog), but I’ll shout out the 2019 Resident Evil 2 remake as something that I really fell in love with over the summer. I’m also really excited about Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, set to launch in about two weeks. That game looks to be, um, about one million hours long.

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

I don’t run every day, but I do love to run as a way to clear my mind, and we’re entering my favorite season to run in. And you know what? Maybe I should run every day.

Thank you, Will, for being the best co-host a boy could ask for. And for not writing about Lost.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

🎙️ Quotations

“I had originally written it about three Black brothers, all of whom are bad guys: a corrupt cop, a drug dealer, and a sexual criminal. And they were all trying to kill each other. And Antoine Fuqua was going to produce it.”

“We sent it out to actors, and no Black actors wanted to play in a movie where there are no good Black people. And it sort of died. But then AI came along, and I didn’t need Black actors.”

-Paul Schrader, director of the upcoming film “Three Guns At Dawn” (via The Playlist)

You can also support us by becoming a 9to5Google Pro member, starting at just $5/month. You get bonus podcast episodes, access to our members-only Discord server, and lots more.

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. Talk to you on Thursday.

-Daniel

title: How do Apple Refurbished products compare with Amazon and Walmart?
snippet: If you’re willing to exercise a little patience rather than rushing out to buy a shiny new Apple product on launch day, then Apple’s refurbished store has always been an excellent option. Typically, there will be around a three-month wait between a product launch and the first refurbished models appearing on Apple’s website. Other companies offers their own alternatives, like Amazon Renewed and Walmart Restored, but it’s important to understand the different standards and warranties that apply … more…
fullText:
If you’re willing to exercise a little patience rather than rushing out to buy a shiny new Apple product on launch day, then Apple’s refurbished store has always been an excellent option. Typically, there will be around a three-month wait between a product launch and the first refurbished models appearing on Apple’s website.

Other companies offers their own alternatives, like Amazon Renewed and Walmart Restored, but it’s important to understand the different standards and warranties that apply …

Apple Certified Refurbished

Buying from Apple’s Certified Refurbished store gets you a typical discount of 15% on a product that will be indistinguishable from new. Specifically, Apple guarantees all of the following:

Full inspection and testing by Apple

A brand new outer shell, so there will never be any marks or scratches

A brand new battery, so you’ll get the same battery life as usual

All original accessories and cables are included

Apple’s standard one-year warranty applies in exactly the same way as a new product

The same eligibility for AppleCare+

Literally the only difference you’ll see is that products are supplied in a plain white box rather than the original packaging.

Amazon Renewed

Amazon Renewed can offer more competitive pricing, but it’s worth being aware that you’re not getting the same guarantees as to condition:

Inspection and testing by the seller, not by Apple

Used outer shell, so expect marks and scratches (see below)

Used battery, only guaranteed to exceed 80% of the original capacity

Accessories may not be genuine Apple ones

90-day Amazon warranty, instead of 1-year Apple one

As for marks and scratches, Amazon offers three tier quality tiers:

Premium/Excellent: No signs of cosmetic damage when held 12 inches away

Good: Light scratches, barely visible when holding the device 12 inches away

Acceptable: Scratches that are easily seen and felt

Walmart Restored

Walmart Restored is a lot vaguer than Amazon on what you’re getting for your money:

Inspection and testing by the seller, not by Apple

No promises as to cosmetic condition, only “like-new performance and reliability”

No specifics on the battery condition beyond the above

No information on accessories

Seller warranty, instead of 1-year Apple one

The seller warranty is for one year on the Restored Premium tier, and 90 days on Like New, Good, and Fair tiers. The company isn’t specific about its definitions for each tier.

9to5Mac’s Take

If you want a product indistinguishable from new in terms of both condition and Apple warranty, then it’s clear that Apple’s refurbished store is the place to go.

Amazon Renewed can, however, offer significantly better pricing, so if you’re willing to accept the compromises listed above, you may consider this a decent deal. In particular, if you’re opting to take our advice to save money by upgrading to the iPhone 17 Pro instead of this year’s model (when the only accessory you’re sacrificing is the cable), there are some attractive deals here:

As for Walmart Restored, I’d worry about the extreme vagueness of the promises, but you do have the option of returning them if you aren’t happy.

title: Reports describe two ways for Apple to make more money; only one is good
snippet: There were two reports in the last few days indicating different routes for Apple to make more money by boosting Services revenue. In my view, it should absolutely do the first of these, but not the second – and it appears Phil Schiller may agree … more…
fullText:
There were two reports in the last few days indicating different routes for Apple to make more money by boosting Services revenue. 

In my view, it should absolutely do the first of these, but not the second – and it appears Phil Schiller may agree …

Let’s start by summarizing the two reports.

Home security & monitoring service

On Friday, Bloomberg suggested that Apple may be planning a new home security and monitoring service to sit alongside some of the new home hardware we’re expecting.

Apple is planning a privacy-centric home security camera and automation device that will use AI to monitor the surrounding environment instead of actual video footage. It will tap into a new home security and monitoring service.

Squeezing more revenue from the App Store

A second report from the same source on Sunday said that the company is looking at ways to squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Ternus and services chief Eddy Cue want to make even more money from the App Store and figure out ways to raise margins and squeeze additional recurring revenue from the platform.

Apple should not take the latter approach

Tackling these in reverse order, I think the second approach would be a very big mistake. 

Apple’s effective monopoly on the sale of iPhone apps has come under fire from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an iPhone app, you are forced to do so through the official App Store, and that leaves you with no choice but to accept the company’s terms on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.

I understand a common view is that nobody forces anyone to buy an iPhone or make apps for it, but that is not the reality of how even the most laissez-faire forms of capitalism work: even the US has had antitrust legislation in place since 1890. When you achieve a certain level of market dominance, then constraints are imposed on how you need to behave in order to ensure you don’t abuse your position.

Trying to squeeze even more money from the App Store is very much the antithesis of skating to where the puck is headed, and Phil Schiller reportedly shares this view as Bloomberg suggests it’s one of the reasons he’s stepped down now.

Schiller, on the other hand, seems to believe that such moves will only further irk developers and governments. While there was no internal blowup or anything like that, it’s something he wanted no part of.

Innovative services are the way to go

Introducing new innovative services that people will want to buy, in contrast, is absolutely the right thing for Apple to do. I can easily see value in the company offering a home security monitoring service.

I argued back in 2024 that making its own smart home camera would be one of the … smartest things the company could do. I said the same again about rumours of an Apple smart doorbell. Adding an optional Services component to security products makes perfect sense for two reasons.

First, there are all the privacy arguments I’ve made before. HomeKit Secure Video has already made a major contribution to ensuring the privacy of security camera feeds. If there is one company I’d trust to perform AI analysis of security camera footage, it’s Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best placed to fully integrate security hardware and services within a HomeKit environment. I’m sure there will be many other areas where Apple can offer similar benefits.

To me, the key is that Apple needs to adopt the same approach to services it does to hardware. Make great products that lead to people willingly parting with their money and doing so with a smile on their face. Not squeezing money in a way that irritates customers, developers, and regulators alike.

title: Group of bipartisan lawmakers ask US government to ban several hack-for-hire firms
snippet: The three Indian companies are accused of using hackers to steal information used to sway litigation.
fullText:
A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers has asked the U.S. government to ban several hack-for-hire firms — companies that carry out cyberattacks on behalf of paying clients. The lawmakers accuse the firms of targeting Americans and abusing foreign courts to silence U.S. reporting on their activities.

Democratic senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, and Republican congressman Pat Harrigan, on Wednesday sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, urging him to add three Indian companies to the department’s economic sanctions “entity list.”

The list effectively bars U.S. businesses from transacting with a named entity, with the aim of restricting the companies from accessing critical technology needed to function, including software licenses and cloud infrastructure. 

In the letter sent to Lutnick and shared with TechCrunch, the lawmakers say BellTroX, CyberRoot, and Sunkissed Organic Farms (which previously operated under its former name, Appin) have for more than a decade conducted cyberattacks and targeted espionage against Americans, business owners, and their lawyers, to “manipulate ongoing litigation.”

The lawmakers say that these mercenary hacking companies have stolen data from thousands of Americans, and accuse the hackers of an “aggressive censorship campaign” to suppress public awareness of their alleged activities.

“This coordinated effort effectively allows foreign entities to use foreign courts to keep the American public in the dark about cyber threats to their own country and undermines the fundamental constitutional rights of U.S. citizens,” the lawmakers said.

It’s not clear if the Commerce Department will add the companies to its entity list, and a spokesperson did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

The letter’s request to add the companies to the entity list follows extensive reporting and media investigations on the hack-for-hire industry, documenting how hackers are paid to break into the inboxes and devices of executives, lawmakers, and military officials to gain an advantage in lawsuits or influence their outcomes.

One of the companies, Appin, previously secured a global court order from an Indian court forcing Reuters to take down its reporting on the company while Reuters appealed the order. The notice that appeared on the page at the time said that Reuters “stands by its reporting.” The order was later lifted and the report republished.

The digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation previously defended two news organizations, Techdirt and the MuckRock Foundation, from legal threats after Appin engaged in “a campaign of bullying and censorship seeking to wipe out stories” about the company’s involvement in mercenary hacking.

The lawmakers’ letter said that the hack-for-hire companies “operated at the behest of the Qatari government” and that their targets included a former senior Republican lawmaker. 

Appin has been linked to Qatar before. Earlier reporting tied Appin to a campaign of cyberattacks against FIFA officials, reportedly directed by Qatar as part of an effort to protect its plans to host the 2022 World Cup. 

A representative from the Qatari government in Washington, D.C. did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

An email from TechCrunch to Anuj Khare, a director at Sunkissed Organic Farms, went unreturned.

Separate reporting by The New Yorker and digital investigative unit The Citizen Lab has also documented espionage activity by the two other hack-for-hire firms named in the lawmakers’ letter, BellTroX and CyberRoot. 

TechCrunch sought comment from representatives at CyberRoot, but did not hear back prior to publication. BellTroX could not be reached for comment.

title: Google Home update fixes alarms, improves media & smart home voice controls
snippet: The latest Google Home update is fixing issues with alarms that some users were experiencing while also improving media and smart home voice controls in Google’s continued effort to address pain points in Gemini for Home. more…
fullText:
The latest Google Home update is fixing issues with alarms that some users were experiencing while also improving media and smart home voice controls in Google’s continued effort to address pain points in Gemini for Home.

The most noticeable upgrade in the latest Google Home update should be around voice commands. On smart speakers and displays, Gemini “now understands a broader range” of commands regarding media and smart home devices. You can also chain commands in the same sentence. 

Google explains:

Expanded capabilities and understanding for media controls: Gemini on speakers and displays now understands a broader range of voice commands across media and home device controls. And, you can now combine media commands with other commands to get things done faster.

Try saying:

“Turn off the lights and stop the music.”

“Skip this song and turn on the backyard lights.”

“Stop captions on this video.”

This update should also fix an issue with Google Keep integration as well as an issue that was preventing users from creating or editing alarms and lists. Seeing as smart speakers and display are very often used as an alarm clock, that’s welcome news.

	

Rounding out this update, the Google Home app should clean up any rogue automations from third-party apps. The automations editor should also be a lot easier to use now, as starters, conditions, and actions are now listed in alphabetical order automatically.

title: Autonomy pivots to gas vehicles to keep the dream of car subscriptions alive
snippet: Scott Painter, founder of TrueCar, is still trying to build a business around vehicle subscriptions, where you can cancel at any time.
fullText:
Four years ago, California startup Autonomy pledged to buy 23,000 EVs from 17 automakers, including Tesla, and make them available as part of a vehicle subscription service. It was a combination of two trends that had taken off in the early 2020s.

It didn’t work out.

Within a year, Autonomy was almost out of business, largely due to an EV price war started by Elon Musk, who was trying to keep Tesla competitive against a rush of new electric vehicles. Autonomy’s fleet, which had barely grown past 1,000 vehicles, lost around a third of its value. Founder Scott Painter (who also created TrueCar) had to more or less bail out the company while major automakers abandoned their own plans for vehicle subscriptions.

The startup has stayed alive, however, and it hasn’t given up on vehicle subscriptions. Instead, Autonomy said on Wednesday that it is adding internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to its fleet for the first time, and is betting the pivot towards a more familiar powertrain will bring in customers.

“If you’re going to be successful in anything, you’ve got to give the customer what the customer wants,” Autonomy’s CEO, Fred Weick, told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “There’s very few examples, I think, in history, of creating things customers didn’t know they wanted.”

The new lineup will feature gas-powered Ford vehicles like the Mustang, Ranger and F-150 pickups, as well as SUVs like the Bronco Sport, Escape and Explorer. Autonomy is sourcing the vehicles from Los Angeles-based Galpin Motors and making them available to customers in California. The company also operates in Arizona, Florida, Texas, New York, North Carolina and Washington, and said it will work with other dealer partners in these markets.

Autonomy is renewing its bet on vehicle subscriptions at a time when new car prices soar above $50,000. Used cars are getting more expensive, too.

Weick, who spent more than 20 years at Mercedes-Benz, said rising prices are making it harder for people with low credit scores — or no access to credit at all — to get a vehicle. His company charges a one-time fee (currently $1,000 for the EVs) and then a set price per month, which varies depending on the make and model. After one month, customers can cancel the subscription at any time.

Weick said Autonomy is targeting four types of customers with this push into ICE vehicles: university students, military families, foreign workers, and people who want a “company car” experience. 

“The crux of the interest is easy and quick access to mobility without all the headaches that come with the old school” way of buying cars, he said. “The past [business] models were all about trying to fit a new concept into old shoes, and that doesn’t work.”

Weick said Autonomy is still seeing interest for EVs, especially in California. The company currently maintains a fleet of a little more than 500 electric cars, which is far from the 23,000 it had promised in 2022. But it’s hardly the only fleet company to have fumbled the transition. Hertz claimed in 2021 that it was going to buy as many as 100,000 Teslas (and more from other automakers), but wound up selling a majority of them in 2024 in favor of gas vehicles.

title: CloudNC raises $20M to automate manufacturing’s most pressing bottlenecks
snippet: UK-based manufacturing software startup CloudNC announced Wednesday a $20 million B extension round, bringing its lifetime total raised amount to $128 million.
fullText:
UK-based manufacturing software startup CloudNC announced a $20 million B extension round on Wednesday, bringing its lifetime total raised amount to $128 million. The company’s last major raise was four years ago, its co-founder and CEO Theo Saville told TechCrunch.

Saville launched CloudNC in 2015 with Chris Emery, now the company’s chief science officer, and offers AI-powered CAM Assist software that automates parts of Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining. CNC is the process of using computer-controlled machines to cut or shape materials precisely into the parts that are then used in automotive, defense, or consumer hardware industries.

Before a part can be cut, Saville said, a machinist or a computer-aided manufacturing programmer has to decide issues like how a part should be held or what tools should be used, Saville said.

They typically use powerful CAM software to help with this ideation phase, and although some of these tools can help users create part features or known part patterns, that’s different from looking at the part and generating an execution strategy an expert would actually want to use. 

“Traditional CAM systems are powerful, but in most workflows, they are still tools that allow programmers to manually specify how a part should be machined,” Saville said. This is where his CAM Assist comes in, a software that plugs into traditional CAM systems, like Autodesk Fusion or Mastercam, to help machinists and programmers make more efficient strategic manufacturing decisions. 

“It selects suitable tools, approach directions, and cutting feeds and speeds, and then drafts the code required to tell the CNC machine what to do,” Saville said. 

Image Credits:CloudNC

From there, the user reviews, edits, and approves the results. Saville said the goal was to help skilled workers be more “efficient and productive,” rather than removing expert judgment from the process. If “traditional CAM is a powerful toolkit,” he said, then “CAM Assist is more like an expert assistant sitting alongside the programmer, automating much of the first-pass thinking and repetitive setup so the human can review, improve, and approve the approach.” 

Saville said more than 1,000 machine shops worldwide use CAM Assist, and 80% of the company’s customer base, which includes both manufacturers and companies, is in the U.S. With a team of 80 employees, the company’s biggest goal is scaling adoption. 

“This makes this the right time to raise additional capital,” he said. Investors in the round include Nimble Ventures, which led the round, Calculus Venture Capital, Entrepreneur First, and LM Capital, Lockheed Martin’s venture arm. “The funding allows us to support wider take-up of CAM Assist, strengthen our go-to-market operations, expand in existing and new markets, and develop new products such as Quote Agent.” 

The premise behind Quote Agent, which targets manufacturers, is similar to CAM Assist. It helps shops assess the estimated cost and risk of a new project so they can move faster to accept — or reject — new work. He tied this somewhat back to geopolitics, pointing to, for example, how machine shops in the U.S. are looking to reshore and how, at the same time, there is a shortage of skilled workers in manufacturing. 

“Machine shops need to quote faster, program faster, and deliver more with the people and machines they already have,” he said, adding that Quote Agent is set to launch next month. 

“There are more ways to machine a typical CNC part than there are atoms in the universe,” he continued. “We have spent years attacking that specific problem, with our own factory, our own software team, and a lot of hard lessons from real machining. It’s been a long process to get to where we are today.”

title: Hands-on: Nothing’s $25 CMF Buds Neo are way better than the price suggests
snippet: Last month, Nothing’s CMF brand launched a new pair of $25 earbuds in the CMF Buds Neo. Too good to be true, I figured, but after getting my hands on them, I’m pleasantly surprised by what they bring to the table despite some expected downsides. more…
fullText:
Last month, Nothing’s CMF brand launched a new pair of $25 earbuds in the CMF Buds Neo. Too good to be true, I figured, but after getting my hands on them, I’m pleasantly surprised by what they bring to the table despite some expected downsides.

The CMF Buds Neo bring a lot to the table on paper. 52-hour battery life, active noise cancellation, some flashy colors, and even dual-device connections alongside support for the Nothing X app and EQ presets. For $25, it’s a compelling package. 

How does it deliver in real life?

I’ve spent a few hours listening to CMF Buds Neo and, honestly, I’m pretty impressed!

	

At their core, they get the job done. The earbuds have decent sound quality, though they’re a bit hollow on default settings. I found that turning down the bass enhancement improves the sound quality, and they’re more optimized for speech (podcasts, etc) than music. Nothing Ear (3a) sound far better; don’t get me wrong, but probably not 4x better as the price on paper suggests.

The sound quality is the most important thing here when the price is so low, and it’s certainly more than good enough to make these a good deal. And there’s clearly more weight put in the price than anything else. CMF Buds Neo have some clear and obvious downsides. The case is cheap-feeling despite looking very nice, and the same goes for the earbuds – the materials feel cheap, but they fit nice in my ear and stay comfortable over a few hours of use. The touchpads on the earbuds are responsive, but lack a play/pause gesture by default. Another downside is the range, as I found these disconnect from my Fold 8 more quickly than other earbuds I’ve tested in recent memory. The case magnets that hold the earbuds in place work well, and there are some nice touches such as a snappy hinge and the lanyard hole on a rotating corner piece. 

There’s also no pairing button on the case, something that will never fail to annoy me, but at least there’s Google Fast Pair – humorously, the Fast Pair pop-up lacks a picture of the earbuds and just says “blue” on the variant I bought.

Downsides are aplenty here, which really shouldn’t come as a surprise. But, at the core, you’re getting earbuds that sound good enough, have most important features, and cost just $25. If you need a spare pair of earbuds to throw in a backpack or at your bedside, or a daily driver on a budget, these are a winner in my book.

title: People’s Picks: 4 Phone Brands Dominate, but 1 Reigns Supreme and It’s Not Apple
snippet: Apple may seem like an obvious winner for most, but readers’ responses say this brand is a force to be reckoned with in the smartphone space.
fullText:
Every few years, you may think about upgrading your smartphone.  A lot of thought and research goes into your next choice, whether it’s the price, features or brand reputation. Maybe you’re eyeing the latest and greatest, or considering a different phone brand or model altogether. Our readers’ opinions may help you decide. 

CNET’s People’s Picks dives into what our readers really think about their tech devices and services, like their internet service provider, TVs and even their mobile carrier. 

This round was all about readers’ phone brands, just in time for Apple’s Sept. 9 Surprise and shine event, where we expect new iPhone models to be revealed. We asked about everything from brand loyalty to battery life, durability and even price-to-value. The results came down to four big-name tech brands. While there’s only one overall winner, other brands win in key categories that can make a big difference in your day-to-day tasks if you’re upgrading soon. 

Overall winner: Google

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Google is the overall winner for CNET’s People’s Picks for Phones. CNET averaged the scores across three categories to determine the overall satisfaction rating, which includes customer satisfaction, battery longevity and price-to-value. 

Google wins with a score of 4.52 out of 5, while Motorola trails closely behind with 4.45. 

“It’s no surprise to me that Google and Motorola scored top marks because both sell some of the most affordable phones that people can buy. Motorola’s Moto G series costs hundreds of dollars less than Apple’s cheapest iPhone,” said CNET’s Director of Content, Patrick Holland. “At $500, Google’s Pixel 10A is one of the best values that you can buy today, especially as phone prices spike due to the ongoing RAM shortage caused by AI and data centers. It just goes to show that in 2026, you can spend less than $500 and still have a great phone that lasts you years.”

On the other hand, Samsung and Apple trail behind with scores of 4.19 and 3.87, respectively. Both brands have evolved in the smartphone space with AI-powered features, upgraded cameras, and thinner phone designs, but fell short in this category. 

“There are a few factors at play here, most notably that Google and Motorola ship a fraction of the phones that Samsung does — so Pixel and Razr buyers are a more devoted core of customers than the many who buy Galaxy phones,” said CNET Managing Editor of Mobile David Lumb. A Counterpoint Research report on phone shipments in the first quarter of 2026 noted that Google (3% of the US market) and Motorola (10%) combined accounted for half of Samsung’s market share (26%). 

The other thing to remember is that Google sells mostly premium phones.

“Aside from the Pixel 10A as a midrange device. Motorola and Samsung have wider ranges of more affordable and cheap phones, so I’d guess there’s less consumer fondness at the lower end of the device price scale,” Lumb said.

Apple’s fourth-place spot is a tougher nut to crack. Perhaps consumers haven’t seen as many upgrades in successive years as they would like in new iPhones, or they’re miffed at the higher prices Apple’s phones sell for. What’s most likely the case, Lumb suggested, is that there are simply more people buying new iPhones. In the Counterpoint report above, Apple handsets accounted for 58% of all phones shipped in the US.

AI features

AI features like photo editing, live translation and AI-powered summaries are becoming the focal point for new smartphone models. But what matters more is how much you’ll use those built-in features. Google Pixel wins with 88% of its users saying their phone’s AI features are essential and occasionally useful.

“Out of the four brands, only one is a true AI company, and that’s Google. In fact, Google’s Gemini AI can run on phones from all four brands, including the iPhone via an app. The Gemini Assistant can be used on Motorola and Samsung phones,” said Holland.

Lumb added that Google has led the charge in both including and promoting AI features in its Pixel phones that people actually use, like Magic Eraser and live translation. 

“Pixel owners have been using AI features for years, and combined with Google aggressively inserting its Gemini assistant throughout the phone, it makes sense that Samsung Galaxy owners would feel a lesser impact from AI.” 

Samsung has made plenty of AI advancements, like a health assistant and browser upgrades, but it falls behind, with only 64% of its users saying the same. Apple and Motorola trail behind with 14% and 8% each. Most Motorola users say the phone lacked built-in tools or ignored them.

What few AI features are available on iPhones were introduced more recently, so it’s unsurprising that their owners wouldn’t consider them essential to daily use, Lumb said. While Gemini continues to evolve, Apple’s advanced AI Siri was delayed for years and will finally launch with the upcoming iOS 27.

Battery life

Ties with Motorola 

For a phone’s battery to exceed expectations, it must last a day or more. Motorola and Google tie in this category, with 74% saying their phones’ batteries exceed expectations by lasting a full day or longer without needing to be charged. Comparatively, Samsung and Apple fall behind, with only about half (52%) saying their phones’ batteries exceed expectations, while others say they just meet expectations. Apple finishes last, with only 31% reporting the same for their iPhones’ batteries. Most said their phone needed to be charged midday. 

“The number one factor for battery life is how you use your phone. And I think this result speaks volumes about how much iPhone owners are on their phones,” said Holland. 

CNET’s phone battery testing found that Apple’s phones had the longest battery life, with OnePlus placing second and Motorola third. However, the test doesn’t account for how you use your phone specifically each day – everyone is different. If you’re hyper-connected and your default is scrolling through social media apps or streaming videos, even the best battery life won’t be enough for you, Holland said. “Thankfully, Google, Motorola and Samsung, along with Apple, have all increased the charging speeds on their handsets to at least make topping them off less of a pain point.”

Motorola 

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Value

Motorola wins in price-to-value, with 82% of its readers saying it offers exceptional value by delivering more than its price suggests. Only 4% rate the brand as overpriced. 

“Before Motorola brought back the Razr as a foldable phone, its most popular handsets were its Moto G line that start as low as $200 and top out at $350,” said Holland. “Motorola has deep, long-term relationships with phone carriers, which often sell these phones at a discount.”

Compared with other brands, 45% of Pixel owners say Google’s phone offers exceptional value, and 35% of Samsung users say the same.

The surprising fact is that Apple places fourth in this category, with 58% of iPhone users saying it’s overpriced. Only 12% find the phone’s value exceptional. However, many tech brands are raising prices due to the RAM shortage, which makes it tough to determine what’s worth the high cost. 

“The only company that hasn’t raised prices on its phones this year is Apple. There’s a chance it might announce a price hike at its Sept. 9 event. The cheapest iPhone the company sells starts at $600. You can find incredible Android phones for less, like the Google Pixel 10A for $500,” said Holland.

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Durability

Choosing a phone that doesn’t shatter, crack or leave you with a broken camera can make a big difference when you need one to last a few years. Some phones are more durable than others. Apple wins this category with 78% of readers saying it’s highly durable against drops and daily use with minimal to no damage. The remaining 22% either deal with normal wear and minor scuffs over time, report their phone as fragile or always have a heavy-duty case to protect it. 

Holland said that when Apple released the iPhone 12 in 2020, it was the first to have a flat, dense build with squared-off sides to increase durability. In the years following, Samsung followed suit, adopting a flat build for its Galaxy S and S Plus models, and Google implemented a similar design with its Pixel phones.

Google follows closely behind with 72% saying their Pixel smartphone is highly durable, while 28% say it’s moderately durable. 

Not as many readers with a Motorola say the phone is highly durable (65%), but even fewer readers with a Samsung (58%) phone say the same. Samsung users say their foldable phone and screens are fragile and only moderately durable. Some readers criticize the brand for the phone’s fragility and susceptibility to damage from drops.

Brand retention and loyalty 

Despite Apple falling short in several categories, 86% of Apple users said they’re extremely likely to buy the same brand next time. 

“Apple’s most popular product is the iPhone, but its iPhone-only features like iMessage and FaceTime, not found on Android, that keep people tied in,” said Holland. “Also, if you want to learn about how to use your iPhone or get it fixed, you can go to the Apple Store and talk with an actual human – I think those retail stores are Apple’s secret weapon.” 

Whereas 79% of Samsung owners share the same sentiment for the brand. Over half of Google Pixel owners (58%) would buy a Google phone again, but only 42% of people with Motorola phones would. Other Motorola owners are using competitor research to determine their next phone purchase.

Methodology 

CNET commissioned Alchemer to conduct the People’s Picks survey to compile data. The survey was carried out online, and all figures are from Alchemer. The total sample comprised 1,107 adults. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus). Fieldwork was undertaken from July 1 to July 28, 2026. 

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Dashia Milden
						

						

							Senior Consumer Insights Editor						
					

											

								

											Dashia is the consumer insights editor for CNET. She specializes in data-driven analysis and news at the intersection of tech, personal finance and consumer sentiment. Dashia investigates economic shifts and everyday challenges to help readers make well-informed decisions, and she covers a range of topics, including technology, security, energy and money. Dashia graduated from the University of South Carolina with a bachelor's degree in journalism. She loves baking, teaching spinning and spending time with her family.

title: Gemini app makes Daily Brief free in the US
snippet: After introducing at I/O 2026 in May, Google is making Daily Brief in the Gemini app available for free in the US. more…
fullText:
After introducing at I/O 2026 in May, Google is making Daily Brief in the Gemini app available for free in the US.

Daily Brief generates a list of your to-dos and priorities every morning. Gemini uses Personal Intelligence to look at your Gmail, Google Calendar, and other Connected Apps, as well as past Gemini chats.

The Daily Brief starts with a “Top of mind” section that shows “timely, actionable items,” such as tasks with upcoming deadlines. “FYI” will show other items that have dates attached. “Looking ahead” is the final section with a focus on long-term goals and “suggested next steps to help you achieve them.”

You can tap on items to “Mark complete” or start a “Chat” with Gemini. There’s also the ability to leave “Helpful” or “Not helpful” feedback.

	

Example use cases include:

For students: Manage class schedules, organize study plans, and track applications.

For entrepreneurs: Surface actionable client emails and update task reminders.

For parents: Manage school communications, track family milestones, and handle household tasks.

For job seekers: Quickly act on recruiter inquiries, prepare for interviews, and monitor application statuses.

As of last Friday, Gemini Daily Brief no longer requires a Google AI subscription in the US. It’s available to personal Google Accounts with Personal Intelligence, Memory, and the Google Workspace integration enabled.

You can access it from the Gemini side panel, with Google also sending a notification every morning. You can disable that alert by going to the account menu and configuring “Notifications.” 

Another way to interact with the digest is through Gemini Live: “What’s my daily brief?”

title: iPhone 18 Pro set to become Apple’s new default model
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro is about to be unveiled, and due to a lineup overhaul this year, it’s set to become Apple’s new default model like never before. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro is about to be unveiled, and due to a lineup overhaul this year, it’s set to become Apple’s new default model like never before.

With no base iPhone 18 available, iPhone 18 Pro will be Apple’s default new model this year

Apple has offered multiple new iPhone models every year for a very long time. And no doubt will for many years to come.

But at this week’s Apple event, a big shakeup is coming to the iPhone lineup.

Rather than launching the typical ‘iPhone’ and ‘iPhone Pro’ options, the base model iPhone 18 will be missing.

Numerous reports point to Apple pushing back the release of iPhone 18 and also iPhone Air 2 into early 2027. That leaves a fall lineup consisting only of:

iPhone 18 Pro

iPhone 18 Pro Max

iPhone Ultra

By delaying iPhone 18 beyond its typical release schedule, iPhone 18 Pro will essentially become Apple’s new default model.

Users who need a cheaper device will still be able to choose from last year’s iPhone 17, or the iPhone 17e or iPhone Air. But in all the marketing we see from Apple and carrier partners this fall and into the holidays, there will be no ‘iPhone 18’ to promote as the new default. Instead, iPhone 18 Pro will fill that role.

iPhone Ultra will be too expensive, and likely fairly niche in comparison.

So for the average person who wants “the new iPhone,” Apple will basically have just two options: iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.

It’s an interesting experiment, and could see iPhone 18 Pro become the new bestselling Pro model. But paired with expected price increases, it’s also a risk for Apple. Prospective upgraders might hold on to their current iPhone longer because there’s no iPhone 18 to upgrade to.

One way or another, we’ll find out very soon whether Apple’s new plan pays off.

title: This Is the Biggest 2D Map of the Universe. Here’s How to Use It
snippet: The map covers 75% of the sky, and you can explore all sorts of cool celestial objects once you know where to look.
fullText:
Scientists have pointed telescopes at the sky and mapped the cosmos for centuries. That relentless pursuit is producing maps that are bigger and more detailed than ever. But there’s one map that stands out above the rest, and now it’s the largest 2D map of the night sky ever created.

The best part? Anyone can play with it. 

The map, called Data Release 11 or DR11, comes courtesy of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team at NSF NOIRLab, headquartered in Tucson, Arizona, with contributions from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California and other agencies and organizations.

Covering 75% of the sky across 5.6 trillion pixels, DR11 is the team’s most comprehensive map to date, built upon prior versions of the same map . It expands on DR9 by 50% and brings back northern sky coverage missing from DR10. Based on 263,407 ground-based exposures by 160 scientists, the map catalogs 4 billion objects — including stars, galaxies, black holes and asteroids — in visible and near-infrared light.

Already cited in over 1,800 research papers, NOIRLab expects this to remain the premier 2D map of its kind for years. According to co-lead David Schlegel, it also laid the groundwork for identifying 60 million targets for the DESI project and for building a full 3D map, which was completed in 2026. With billions of targets still unstudied, Schlegel told CNET that “plenty of other discoveries” remain hidden in plain sight for public exploration.

Enough talk, let’s play

The map covers 75% of the night sky, with the black swath through the middle obscured by black holes, interstellar dust and other obstacles.Legacy Survey

The map doesn’t look like much at first. But if you pick a spot and start zooming in, you can get a pretty good idea of how vast it really is. What appears to be a cloud of pretty colors is actually billions of objects floating around in space.

You might notice that DR11, which is designed to see out into the universe, doesn’t contain any planets, moons or asteroids within our solar system. That may be a little bit of a bummer for some, but there are plenty of other objects to look for.

Though the user interface is a little overwhelming at first, you really only need four boxes to play around — and all four of them are right next to each other in the bottom-left corner. 

Zoom: This indicates how zoomed in you are based on the +/- slider on the top left. It goes from degrees to arc minutes and then finally to arc seconds. I got most of my best results between 20 and 50 arc minutes. 

Contrast and brightness: Below zoom, you’ll find the contrast slider, which reduces the background noise of the map. Under that, the brightness slider helps illuminate smaller objects. Adjust these settings as needed to get the best view, but start with the defaults.

Jump to object: This is the most important box, where you can type in the names of celestial bodies to find them on the map. I searched for a couple dozen celestial objects, and found them all pretty quickly. Online lists of named black holes, quasars and other cool celestial bodies can be a good starting point in exploring the universe — I have more tips for finding them if you keep reading.  

Once you land on something, use the zoom slider in the top-left corner to zoom in and get a closer look. (Don’t use your mouse wheel for this because it zooms in wherever your pointer is, potentially taking you to a completely different part of the map.) You can also drag the cursor around the screen to view everything around the object you’re looking at.

A sky like you’ve never seen it

Arcturus is comparably huge in the night sky, and so it is also comparably huge on the map.Legacy Survey

My first visit on the map was to Arcturus, the fourth-largest star in the sky. Zoomed in, it’s much larger than every other object around it by a rather wide margin, which is why it’s so easy to find in the night sky. 

Another search took me to LHS 1140b, the first star ever discovered that sits in another star’s habitable zone with an atmosphere. This one is much smaller than Arcturus and required me to zoom in to 30 arc seconds to see it. It’s quite close to its host star, which makes sense since the habitable zone is pretty close to the star itself. Earth would appear at a similar distance from the sun if viewed from this perspective. 

The star that LHS 1140b orbits is also dimmer than many other stars. It’s about 20% the size of the sun, so it almost looks like a big planet rather than a small star.

This binary star system hosts planet HD 80606 b, a planet known to orbit so close to its star that it is scorched. It’s so close, in fact, that the light from the binary star system hides it completely.Legacy Survey

Some stuff is easier to find than others. For example, planet HD 80606 b is so close to its star that it is absolutely scorched, with temperature swings of 1,100 degrees Fahrenheit. Bright glare from its binary stars completely obscures HD 80606 b on the map. It’s still there, though, getting blasted by its star like a blowtorch caramelizing sugar on the top of a crème brûlée.

You’ll notice that the map has a large, sweeping blank spot running through it. These are the parts of the sky that haven’t been mapped yet. Researchers say that this is due to various obstacles, such as space dust, bright stars getting in the way of scans and black holes covering everything behind them. 

For example, try searching for Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. The map shows you where it is — right inside one of those blank bands. The black hole prevents any telescope from seeing the stars and planets behind it, so that part of the map remains blank. 

More advanced options

The planet LHS 1140b orbits a star about one-fifth the size of our sun, and is one of the better candidates for a planet hosting life. Legacy Viewer

You’ll also see a box with a ton of options in the top-right corner of the map. For basic viewing, you don’t have to interact with this box at all, but there are some fun things in there if you want to see them. 

Images: This dropdown menu lets you select which set of images you want to use. Leave that on Legacy Surveys DR11 because that’s the most recent dataset. 

Overlays: This menu is more complicated, as it includes a lot of different datasets you can overlay. Many of them just show which telescopes, instruments and surveys found each separate part of the map. You can leave them all off and still search around the universe for cool stuff. 

However, there is one set of overlays that is worth your time: the Bright objects overlay, with options that actually help you navigate the map. For example, the Bright stars option will put blue circles around the brightest stars on the map with names, making them much easier to find. That’s how I learned that the designation for Arcturus is HR 5340.

Bright objects include star clusters, planetary nebulae and some more specific ones — but the most fun is the Constellations overlay, which shows off every constellation in the sky. If you toggle it on, pick a constellation and zoom into each corner and point, you can find the bright stars that humans used to construct these constellations ages ago. 

Finding stuff to search for

Constellations such as Ursa Minor can be seen on the 2D map, letting you explore the bright stars that make up their shape.Legacy Survey

The real challenge in using the DR11 app is figuring out what to look up. There are all sorts of celestial bodies, and many of them have some pretty cool stories. However, there really isn’t much of a repository to find these things.

We know AI isn’t great at many things, but Schlegel suggested that a large language model may be pretty good for this application since it can scan the web quickly. 

This isn’t without its caveats. Schlegel said that Google Gemini tends to “spit out sexagesimal coordinates” that don’t work in the map’s viewer website because they’re an archaic sky-mapping system. However, Anthropic’s Claude uses decimal-degree coordinates, which work. While the team is looking into supporting both, Schlegel said he prefers the newer decimal system over the archaic system originally invented by Hipparchus and Ptolemy.

The team also gave CNET a list of some pretty neat stuff to look up in the map viewer if you need more ideas. These are some of the most gorgeous pieces of imagery on the entire map: 

NGC 5272 – The Globular Cluster

NGC 4826 – The Black Eye Galaxy

NGC 3351 – The Barred Spiral Galaxy

NGC 4486 – Virgo A

NGC 5457 – The Pinwheel Galaxy

NGC 4594 – Sombrero Galaxy

Schlegel also recommended visiting an FAQ web page for more granular guidance on using the search and overlay functions to improve your experience.

title: Xbox Game Pass will get a Google TV app ‘in the coming months,’ likely only for TCL
snippet: Following a prior teaser that was the better part of a year ago, Microsoft has finally acknowledged its work on a Google TV app for Xbox Game Pass on TCL TVs, but it’s still “months” out from the sound of it. more…
fullText:
Following a prior teaser that was the better part of a year ago, Microsoft has finally acknowledged its work on a Google TV app for Xbox Game Pass on TCL TVs, but it’s still “months” out from the sound of it.

TCL first announced that an Xbox Game Pass app would be coming to its TVs – the Google TV models, specifically – back at CES 2026. That was in January. Microsoft never acknowledged the announcement publicly, and it’s been months since we’ve gotten any updates.

Today, Microsoft has officially confirmed that it will release an Xbox Game Pass app on TCL TVs, marking the first time the cloud gaming service will officially be available on Google TV. Microsoft’s announcement never formally acknowledges Google TV by name, hinting that this is probably exclusive to TCL TVs, rather than being available for the broader platform. TCL is the biggest Google TV partner and, while it also produces Roku and Fire TV units, it primarily uses Google TV and had previously teased the Xbox app directly around its new Google TV flagship.

But the Xbox Game Pass app for TCL’s Google TV sets is apparently still “months” away, despite the nine-month gap we’ve already gone through since the collaboration was first announced.

	

Microsoft says:

Today, we’re sharing a new partnership with TCL that will bring the XBOX app to select TCL Smart TVs in the coming months…

…With the XBOX app on supported TCL Smart TVs, players will be able to access XBOX Cloud Gaming through their Game Pass subscription to stream supported games directly from their TV. For eligible XBOX Game Pass subscribers, that means access to an instant library of games spanning blockbuster releases, beloved franchises, and indie favorites through their cloud playtime.

This comes just a day after Microsoft announced major changes to its cloud gaming setup on Xbox Game Pass. Players will now have a limited number of hours per month, topping out at 15 hours, before they need to pay more.

title: Apple making just a few hundred iPhone Ultras per day, per report
snippet: We’re less than a week away from Apple announcing its first-ever foldable iPhone. A new supply chain report today says that Apple’s “extremely high quality control standards” have led to a much slower ramp for iPhone Ultra production so far. more…
fullText:
We’re less than a week away from Apple announcing its first-ever foldable iPhone. A new supply chain report today says that Apple’s “extremely high quality control standards” have led to a much slower ramp for iPhone Ultra production so far.

iPhone Ultra production status 

According to Nikkei Asia, Apple is currently making “a few hundred” iPhone Ultra units per day. This could make it “challenging” for Apple to meet market demand for the device. 

The report says that Apple added an extra trial run of iPhone Ultra production in August to “ensure the phone can be mass-produced according to its specified design.” This decision reportedly delayed actual commercial production of the device “for weeks.”

In particular, Apple is said to be focused on improving the production yields of the “surface flatness and the performance of the hinge.”

The current situation, according to Nikkei’s sources, could result in limited availability of the iPhone Ultra when sales of the device begin. “Normally, tens of thousands of phones would need to be produced each day to meet the planned production goal for the foldable iPhone,” the report says.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported this week that he expects the foldable iPhone to be released “at the same time or very close to it” as the iPhone 18 Pro models. Gurman said that he doesn’t believe there are “massive delays or supply chain issues” impacting the device at this point.

Apple is expected to announce the iPhone Ultra on Wednesday next week as part of its “Surprise and shine” special event. Other rumored announcements include AirPods 5, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, and iPhone 18 Pro. What are you most excited to see? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Hackers are stealing Claude tokens from subscribers
snippet: Last month, a Claude user noticed his account was consuming tokens even though he wasn't working. Anthropic has since warned users about hackers.
fullText:
On August 4, Grant De Swardt, an independent AI consultant in East Sussex, U.K., noticed something strange going on with his Claude Max 20x account. He hadn’t been working that day, yet his token usage was climbing.

The next day, he disabled everything he had attached to Claude and did not work with it. Token consumption again increased. “In the clearest controlled interval, it increased from 45% to 55% while I performed no work, scheduled Cowork tasks were paused or completed, Dispatch/cloud execution was disabled, and there was no corresponding active local Claude Code task,” De Swardt told TechCrunch.

What was eating up his token allowance? He had no idea, so he contacted Anthropic and asked for an itemized list. Anthropic didn’t provide one, but it agreed something was off. It suspended his paid account, invalidated all of his sessions and server-side Claude Code tokens, and issued him a partial refund of £44.49 for the remaining time on his $200-per-month subscription.

The suspension wreaked havoc on his business, he told TechCrunch. His job is to help small and mid-size businesses set up agents — a sort of forward-deployed engineer for hire — for tasks like automatically loading purchase-order data from emails into the accounting software.

As a sole proprietor, he relies on agents throughout his whole business, too: daily admin tasks, website design, coding. “Like everything is just running through AI these days,” he said.

After investigating, Anthropic told De Swardt it found the culprit: A compromised Claude session key was used to mint unauthorized Claude Code OAuth tokens. The company told him the account “appeared to have been used by an unauthorized-looking third-party service to handle activity for other people, but they could not determine how it obtained access,” he told TechCrunch. “They say the evidence is consistent either with credentials/session data being taken without my knowledge, or with the account having been connected to an outside service.”

In other words, a hacker was able to obtain access to De Swardt’s account and was covertly siphoning off his tokens. Because account support tracks total usage but not itemized usage, even upon request, this kind of theft could have gone on for months undetected.

He posted his experience on Reddit and after 80 comments, he discovered he was not alone. One person claimed that their account “was auto-upgraded without my consent, my credit card got charged, and the usage shot from 0% to 100% automatically without me even touching it.” Another saw usage go from 0 to 49% in 12 minutes, when all they had used it for was a couple of prompts and a web search.

One Claude user said their account burned through its max tokens every day for three days without them using it at all; this person then created a GitHub report about it. Like with the Reddit post, other users shared similar experiences there, too.

Two of them posted emails from Anthropic where the company had — to its credit — identified and warned them that their tokens were being stolen.

“We have recently become aware of a bad actor that is using common infostealer malware to steal Claude login sessions from people’s computers, then using those login sessions to access Claude accounts and consume their usage,” the email read. Infostealers are a type of malware that installs itself on a user’s computer and steals saved passwords, session data, and login credentials.

When Anthropic saw suspicious activity, it signed the users out, invalidated existing authorizations, issued some refunds, and warned them that they may have malware.

The company also said the malware didn’t come from using Claude itself. Such malware can be picked up from many sources online, from downloading infected software to clicking on infected ads.

Anthropic did not send De Swardt one of those emails. He insists he found no evidence that his computer was compromised and says he still has no way of determining how hackers gained access.

De Swardt’s Claude account was reinstated after about two weeks. But the difficulty of getting speedy help for the matter, plus the lack of an itemized usage, soured him on Claude. He cancelled his subscription in favor of Cursor and its ability to use multiple models, including more affordable open source options.

In his experience, these other models work as well as Claude. “It’s not that much different or better,” he said, adding that he can’t see going back “without [Anthropic] actually having resolved the issue in any way.” 

He says Anthropic still lacks tools that allow users to see what’s consuming their tokens. “I don’t think there’s any way that these people can protect themselves.”

When asked for information on how users can identify misuse, Anthropic declined to comment.

title: Rivian spinout Also apologizes for delays in shipping futuristic e-bikes
snippet: Rivian's futuristic e-bike is delayed, and customers are not happy. fullText:
Rivian’s futuristic e-bike is delayed, and customers are not happy.

Last year, Rivian’s micromobility spinoff Also unveiled a new, software-controlled electric bike called the TM-B that immediately set the e-bike world ablaze. With USB-C chargeable battery, removable seat post, and software-controlled pedal-by-wire system, the TM-B set itself apart with a totally unique approach to electric bicycle design. It’s not an exaggeration to say that nothing else looked like this bike.

But that list of high-tech features is creating unexpected bottlenecks for Also’s product team. The company had originally said customer deliveries would start in spring 2026, and then later summer. But now, with fall approaching, the TM-B has yet to reach any customers — and several reservation holders are making their frustrations with the delays known on Reddit.

This past weekend, Also went the unique route of responding to those criticisms on Reddit. Saul Leiken, Also’s product manager, posted a 661-word letter apologizing to customers for the delays, attributing the hold-up to strict quality standards rather than rushing an unfinished product.

Leiken attributes the delay to “significant supply chain challenges” as a result of the AI boom. Specifically, the company has struggled to find enough printed circuit board (PCB) and integrated circuit (IC) materials for its software-powered e-bike. In some cases, Also’s team has had to find new materials that deviate from the original design, which requires more engineering and testing work to make sure its the right fit.

TM-B’s battery has also presented some hurdles. The batteries, which are available in either 538Wh or 808Wh packs, are supposed to offer up 100 miles of range. But the 240W power delivery exceeds current regulatory guidelines, which is forcing Also to work with standards groups to establish “new safety and testing protocols,” Leiken says.

Lastly, Also may have bitten off more than it can chew with the DreamRide drivetrain system. It’s a pedal-by-wire system, which means there’s no mechanical connection between the pedaling and the movement of the bike. Instead, the rider pedals a generator motor on the crank, which replenishes the battery; a separate traction motor at the rear wheel is software-driven via a Gates Carbon belt drive. But the system requires “high-precision manufacturing,” Leiken admits, which has led to “a slower production ramp-up to ensure quality.”

Rivian’s Also set out to build one of the most high-tech, complex e-bikes ever made. So it shouldn’t necessarily come as a shock to anyone that it’s taking a while to get the manufacturing and production process just right. You could certainly argue that Rivian should have been more clear-eyed about the challenges it would likely face given the complexity of the bike. And to his credit, Leiken does admit they could have done a better job at communicating those delays to customers, and for that he apologizes.

“With any complex and technology-laden product, we have a choice,” he said. “As we ramp production we can relax standards against an original timeline or we can hold to a high standard and face potential delays. We believe our decision to hold that standard was, and is, the right one. And, at the same time, we agree that we should have been more communicative along the way.”
