title: No iPhone Ultra today? Three possible explanations …
snippet: It was widely expected that the first foldable iPhone set to be launched later today would be named the iPhone Ultra. However, a report yesterday said that the device will instead be called the iPhone Duo. If accurate, it’s an interesting development as it might potentially point to the company reserving the Ultra suffix for a completely different future model … more…
fullText:
It was widely expected that the first foldable iPhone set to be launched later today would be named the iPhone Ultra. However, a report yesterday said that the device will instead be called the iPhone Duo.

If accurate, it’s an interesting development as it might potentially point to the company reserving the Ultra suffix for a completely different future model … 

Opinion pieces in which I muse about possible future developments are by their very nature speculative, and this one perhaps more than most. When it comes to hard facts, the only thing we can say for sure is that Apple has used the Ultra label to mean the top-level offering in three contexts:

Apple Watch Ultra

Apple Silicon chips (eg. M5 Ultra)

CarPlay Ultra

It’s been speculated that the company plans to expand the use of the Ultra moniker to a range of new products. This was expected to include the iPhone Ultra and the MacBook Ultra.

Specifically, the iPhone Ultra label was reportedly going to be used for the foldable phone being launched later today. As of yesterday, however, we are expecting this to be named the iPhone Duo – so what’s up? I can see three possibilities.

1. The least interesting reason

The least interesting explanation would be that Apple isn’t using the Ultra label because the foldable phone isn’t the ultimate iPhone. It’s a device with a unique feature, but it’s expected to be inferior to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in several ways. If all the reports pan out, it won’t have a variable aperture lens on the main camera, and will also lack a telephoto camera; it won’t have Face ID; and it won’t match the battery life of the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Logically then, it shouldn’t be called the iPhone Ultra. But Apple hasn’t always followed the logic when it comes to product names – for example, the MacBook Air weighing more than the 12-inch MacBook back in 2015, and the Mac Studio being more powerful than the Mac Pro in 2022. So while this is one possible explanation, it’s far from a definitive one.

2. The Ultra will be the 20th anniversary model

A related possibility is that the iPhone Ultra label is slated for the 20th anniversary model expected next year, taking a significant step closer to that long-term ‘single slab of glass’ vision. If that combined the slickest design with iPhone Pro capabilities, then that would indeed be worthy of the name.

3. There’s something even bigger in the works

The most exciting possibility is that Apple won’t be done with all-new additions to the iPhone range after the launch of the slab of glass (iPhone Glass?), and that the iPhone Ultra label is being reserved for a completely different model – one that really would sit at the top of the lineup in every respect.

I won’t get into speculation about what form that might take, though it will surprise nobody when I say my own hopes would center around significantly superior camera capabilities, starting with a much larger sensor. 

Where do you stand? Which of the three explanations do you think most likely? Or do you have a better idea of your own? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Motorola is finally making a new Wear OS watch and it’s not called the Moto 360
snippet: It’s finally happening. Motorola is making a new Wear OS smartwatch, but it’s not a new Moto 360 – this is the Moto Watch Ultra. more…
fullText:
It’s finally happening. Motorola is making a new Wear OS smartwatch, but it’s not a new Moto 360 – this is the Moto Watch Ultra.

Rewinding the clock, the Moto 360 is perhaps still the most iconic Android smartwatch of all time. It was the poster child for the early days of “Android Wear,” but Motorola threw in the towel after a couple of generations. There was a brief revival of the Moto 360 name in 2020, but even that faded away – and the licensing deal behind it is likely why Motorola isn’t using that name now.

Motorola hasn’t stopped making smartwatches in that time, but they’ve all been based on an RTOS, making them fall into the category of smartwatches that are focused on health tracking and battery life at the expense of more useful notifications and access to a proper app ecosystem. The most recent attempt ended up cloning Wear OS’ design, despite the limitations.

Now, Motorola has a new smartwatch – the Moto Watch Ultra.

	

The $349 smartwatch offers up a Snapdragon W5+ Gen 1 chipset, 2GB of RAM, and 32GB of storage, all used to power Wear OS 6. We’ll have to wait and see if Motorola has made any customizations to the UI here, but re-entering the Wear OS ecosystem is a pretty big deal. Motorola does note that its Qira AI assistant is on board.

The Ultra has a 1.5-inch pOLED display in a 46mm chassis that’s 12.1mm thick – though Motorola’s images make it seem a lot thicker. The display is covered in Gorilla Glass 3 and the body is stainless steel with a brushed finish in silver or gunmetal finishes. There are four strap options, including both silicone and leather, but you can use any 22mm band as there are no fancy connectors, just a traditional spring pin. There’s NFC support for Google Wallet, IP68 + 5ATM dust/water resistance, and LTE support too. Motorola claims 2 days of use from the 550 mAh battery inside – Pixel Watch 5 (45mm) has a 465 mAh battery, for comparison. Charging is handled by a magnetic dock that connects over USB-C.

On the fitness side, Motorola is working with Polar – another brand that tried and has since left the Wear OS market – with features including activity goals, scores, and intensity zones, as well as inactivity alerts, energy sources, and wellness features around breathing and sleep. 

The Moto Watch Ultra will be available unlocked starting on September 10 for $349, with a debut on Verizon on September 24. Other carriers including T-Mobile, Metro, and AT&T will follow later on. 

Beyond the Watch Ultra, Motorola is today also launching a Swarovski version of the base Razr (2026). This special release has the same specs, but with a new dark grey case that has Crystals by Swarovski embedded in the back. It also costs $100 more at $899 and is also launching on September 10.

title: Girl Scouts Unleash Treats for Dogs and Allergy-Safe Cookies for Humans
snippet: You won’t be able to buy Patch Pals and Sparkables from your neighborhood Girl Scout, however.
fullText:
Girl Scout cookie season doesn’t start until January, but when it arrives, two new cookies will appeal to groups who likely haven’t been able to indulge in Girl Scout cookies before: people with dietary restrictions, and dogs.

Sparkables, a crunchy, allergy-friendly oatmeal cookie with chocolate chips and rainbow sprinkles, is formulated for those who are nut-free, gluten-free and vegan. They were developed with Partake Foods, and include whole-grain oats, organic brown sugar, semisweet chocolate chips, cassava flour, oat flour, white rice flour and more. See the full ingredient list online.

Sparkables are meant to include people with food allergies in Girl Scout cookie season.Girl Scouts of the USA

Patch Pals, a soft-baked, blueberry muffin-flavored treat specifically for pups, was developed with the pet-product company Bark. The treats, which feature four designs representing iconic Girl Scout patches, are for dogs who weigh more than 5 pounds and are older than 6 months. Nutritional info and other details available online.

Sparkables and Patch Pals will only be sold online, so you can’t order them from Girl Scouts outside your local store. The new varieties will be available for shipping when Girl Scout cookie season launches on Jan. 12. You can sign up now to receive a reminder when that date comes.

title: This new reveal suggests MacBook Ultra might cost more than we think
snippet: As soon as next month, Apple is expected to introduce its next MacBook Pro redesign. We’ll be seeing OLED, the first touchscreen on a Mac, a thinner chassis, Dynamic Island, and much more. This upgrade was rumored to be called MacBook Ultra, though it wasn’t necessarily clear where that’d leave the MacBook Pro brand. Now, it’s a lot more clear. more…
fullText:
As soon as next month, Apple is expected to introduce its next MacBook Pro redesign. We’ll be seeing OLED, the first touchscreen on a Mac, a thinner chassis, Dynamic Island, and much more. This upgrade was rumored to be called MacBook Ultra, though it wasn’t necessarily clear where that’d leave the MacBook Pro brand. Now, it’s a lot more clear.

At first, one would’ve assumed that the base model 14″ MacBook Pro with the M5 chip would fulfill the MacBook Pro moniker. Then, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple would also be bringing certain elements of the MacBook Ultra design to the base MacBook Pro with M7. To me, this made the idea of ‘MacBook Ultra’ branding much less likely.

Now, a new report makes the idea of both MacBook Pro and MacBook Ultra much more sensible in the lineup.

According to Omdia, Apple will be keeping the current miniLED display panels in production through 2028.

This means two things: for one, if the existing MacBook Pro is staying in the lineup, the redesigned model will likely come with a significant price premium. It also means that the new model is much more likely to be called MacBook Ultra.

So, over the course of the next ~year, the MacBook lineup will likely look like this:

Fall 2026:

MacBook Neo (A18 Pro)

MacBook Air (13-inch and 15-inch, M5)

MacBook Pro (miniLED, 14-inch, M6)

MacBook Pro (miniLED, 14-inch and 16-inch, M5 Pro and M5 Max)

MacBook Ultra (OLED, 14-inch and 16-inch, M5 Pro and M5 Max)

Spring 2027:

MacBook Neo (A19 Pro)

MacBook Air (13-inch and 15-inch, M6)

MacBook Pro (OLED, 14-inch, M7)

MacBook Pro (miniLED, 14-inch and 16-inch, M5 Pro and M5 Max)

MacBook Ultra (OLED, 14-inch and 16-inch, M5 Pro and M5 Max)

Wrap up

If all comes to fruition, the MacBook lineup will be bigger than ever. Ultimately, the older MacBook Pro remaining in the lineup will probably be short lived. I imagine it’s part of Apple’s strategy to keep the starting prices lower, as the company has done in the past. 

	

In this scenario, I could see the miniLED MacBook Pros remaining around at $2499 starting, whereas the Ultra starts even higher, perhaps $2999.

title: Hands-on: Honor’s Robot Phone is probably the coolest phone you still can’t buy
snippet: Decked out with a gimbal and shockingly good camera, the Robot Phone is one of the weirdest devices to come out of Honor. Even if you ignore the fact that it’s limited to China, Honor can’t keep up with demand. more…
fullText:
Decked out with a gimbal and shockingly good camera, the Robot Phone is one of the weirdest devices to come out of Honor. Even if you ignore the fact that it’s limited to China, Honor can’t keep up with demand.

When Honor began teasing a device that hid a fully functional gimbal and a 200MP camera tucked away in its camera bar, it truly seemed like an AI-driven fever dream of what future phones might look like.

Having played around with one this past week, I’m not distancing myself from that thought. Still, I can’t deny it’s a ridiculously cool idea, and a now fully functional Android phone the company launched last month.

Honor’s Robot Phone is aimed at creators more than anyone, for obvious reasons. The 200MP camera sits inside the device’s camera bar, which shouldn’t get you any weird looks if you use it in its retracted form. But as soon as you hit a certain dedicated camera app button and move the physical protective cover, that massive camera rises out of the Robot Phone’s rear panel as if it belonged in a horror movie.

	

The additional 50MP ultrawide and 200MP periscope camera do not move.

The camera app leaves controls up to the user, with full pan/tilt controls and a wide range to cover just about anything in view. It can be flipped 180 degrees for selfie capture, or used outward to record or capture the world in front of you.

Beyond that, Honor has packed some really cool film tools and recording formats. There are panning options and automatic spin controls to get neat shots you’d need to be really skilled to get with your regular old phone. The phone, being a product of Honor’s focus on AI, has object and person tracking. It works better than I anticipated during my short time with the phone, and stabilization was shockingly good for what is, again, a gimbal attached to a phone.

Its bag of tricks is huge, and it was a ton of fun to play around with. Honor pushes a little beyond simple camera tools with the AI-assisted mode, which is what some of the earliest teasers for the phone showcased. MagicOS has an AI assistant named “YOYO,” and it charges it with the ability to look around and gather digital information like a pair of smart glasses would.

It has its struggles when asking it questions in English instead of Chinese, but it’s a neat concept if a little unsettling.

Beyond the camera tools and mechanical gimbal, the Robot Phone brings many of the standard feature sets MagicOS 10 builds out for the manufacturer’s other devices. Overall, it’s a fun and interesting concept that deserves a ton of credit in what can often be a monotonous phone landscape.

At RMB 9,999 – nearly $1,500 – Honor’s Robot Phone is priced well, all things considered. That’s the running price for the 12/512GB configuration. The 16GB/1TB model nears $2,000.

But you probably couldn’t buy it if you wanted to. On top of being launched for the Chinese market with no global launch expected, Honor shared that the device reached sales targets almost immediately. It seemingly kept expectations low, and now has to catch up with demand while supplies are difficult to get a hand on for reasonable prices.

Again, I only messed around with the Robot Phone for a short time, but it ended up being one of those hands-on sessions that reminded me phones can be exceptionally fun. I’m not saying every phone should have an extending gimbal and overkill camera setup, but it’s kind of cool that the option exists – even if heavily limited.

title: Where Google Wallet state IDs are available on Android
snippet: States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android. more…
fullText:
States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android.

Update 9/5

How to add your state ID on Android

Open the Google Wallet app on Android 9+

Tap the “plus” button next to “View more” at the bottom

Choose “ID & personal info” and then “Driver’s license or state ID” 

Select your state and follow the instructions

The process involves taking a picture of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of yourself for verification: a “photo from this video will be submitted to your ID issuer.” 

Once approved, the ID will appear below the carousel of payment methods alongside other passes. The order can be rearranged, while you can remotely remove the ID online if your phone is missing: myaccount.google.com > Personal Info > Manage IDs.

	

What Google Wallet state IDs are supported

Arizona (Rolled out October 2023)

Arkansas (Rolled out October 2025)

California (Rolled out August 2024)

Colorado (Rolled out October 2023)

Georgia (Rolled out October 2023)

Iowa (Rolled out June 2025)

Maryland (Rolled out December 2022)

Montana (Rolled out August 2025)

New Mexico (Rolled out December 2024)

North Dakota (Rolled out October 2025)

[New] Ohio (Rolled out September 2026)

Puerto Rico (Rolled out October 2025)

Where state IDs are coming next

Google previously said to expect support in the following places:

West Virginia (Upcoming availability announced April 2025)

Where you can use state IDs

The primary place you can use this digital ID is at TSA checkpoints in some US airports. There are two ways to do so, starting with tapping your phone at the NFC terminal. You then review the information that will be shared with the TSA and authenticate with device unlock. There’s also a QR code method that requires opening the ID in Google Wallet. 

Officially, you still have to carry the physical ID card at all times.

Some apps, like from car rental services, are beginning to accept digital IDs for identity and age verification. On mobile, if an app or website requests your age, it’s as simple as confirming (and authenticating) that you want to share this information with a system-level prompt/sheet. On desktop web, the experience involves scanning a QR code. 

Google wants to make it possible to do that “without any possibility to link back to a user’s personal identity” through what it calls Zero-Knowledge Proof. This technology will be open-sourced for anyone to use. 

Looking ahead, the IDs can be used at DMVs in Arizona, Georgia, Maryland, and New Mexico as part of “improved and streamlined customer experiences.”

	

Google is also working on letting you use digital IDs to “recover Amazon accounts, access online health services with CVS and MyChart by Epic, verify profiles on platforms like Uber and more.”

Using passport as REAL ID

Google in April pointed out how you can “use your ID pass created from a U.S. passport with TSA security for domestic travel at supported airports, even if you do not have a REAL ID driver’s license or state-issued ID.” This comes ahead of the May 7, 2025 deadline. 

To do so, open Google Wallet > Add to Wallet > ID pass. This three-step process involves taking a picture of your passport’s info page, and then scanning the security chip found inside the back cover of your passport. You also have to record a video of your face that Google will review “to make sure you’re a real person, and compare the video to your passport photo to make sure you’re the owner of the passport.”

The NFC and QR code instructions for using this digital passport ID are unchanged from above. You also have to keep the physical version on you when traveling. As a reminder, this won’t work internationally.

title: The Exploration Company nabs $450 million to challenge SpaceX
snippet: The Exploration Company (TEC) has raised $450 million to build reusable spacecraft, in what it describes as “the largest-ever Series C by a European space company.”
fullText:
The queue to send objects into orbit is growing, but space infrastructure isn’t keeping up with demand. As the realization sinks in that Elon Musk’s SpaceX can’t be the sole answer, other companies are raising their hand — and money.

These include The Exploration Company (TEC), which operates out of Germany, France, Luxembourg, Spain, and Italy, and which has raised $450 million in what it describes as “the largest-ever Series C by a European space company.” But the race is global, with U.S.-based rival Stoke Space currently raising a $1 billion Series E round.

Rivalry aside, these rounds show that investors on both sides of the Atlantic are willing to back companies seeking to build reusable spacecraft. That’s a category pioneered by SpaceX, but that many players, both public and private, now believe it shouldn’t solely control as space gains strategic importance.

These sovereignty-related concerns create extra tailwinds for an EU-headquartered company like TEC. Led by Hélène Huby, a French national who spent two decades at Airbus and ArianeGroup, the company intends to use its funding to build the foundation for a reusable European heavy-lift launcher offering an affordable alternative to SpaceX.

SpaceX itself may have no other choice but to loosen its nascent monopoly on low-earth-orbit launches to prioritize its own payloads; reports suggest that its Falcon rockets are already increasingly reserved for its Starlink satellites, amid uncertainty as to what will happen when these get retired in favor of Starship.

This creates demand that TEC won’t be able to meet for years, even if it sticks to its self-admittedly ambitious timeline. According to Atomico, “10 Nyx missions are booked,” with “more than $2 billion in contracts and commitments.”

Some of these commitments come from institutional partners, including the European Space Agency, but also NASA. Its Series C was also transatlantic, with Atomico, and the EQT-managed Scaleup Europe Fund co-leading the round alongside Bessemer Venture Partners, whose partner Alex Ferrara will join TEC’s board of directors. 

This latest round also consolidates TEC’s status as a company mostly funded by private investors, and one that plans accordingly. In a press conference earlier today, Huby said that she’d love to see Europe add human space flight to its roadmap, but wouldn’t be able to convince VCs to spend $4 billion towards a crew capsule, “then wait 10 years.”

So, TEC’s timeline is more pragmatic, but it is tight. Its most immediate focus is Nyx, a reusable capsule akin to SpaceX’s Dragon and capable of carrying cargo, then people. The company intends to get Nyx to dock with the soon-to-be-retired International Space Station and return safely to Earth by November 2028.

According to Huby, funding from the Series C will stretch to also fund Storm, a rocket engine program paving the way for further developments, at least initially. “Where we need more money is to build a launch pad, and to build the rocket itself,” she told journalists.

TEC wouldn’t be the first European commercial space company to launch a rocket — German startup Isar Aerospace crossed that milestone out of Norway last weekend. Huby praised the feat as “great news for the whole ecosystem,” but said that TEC intends to build a much bigger rocket than Isar’s expandable Spectrum vehicle.

However, Isar also has “a much bigger” launch vehicle in its roadmap, Ars Technica reported — presumably for the same reason Huby gave as to why TEC does. “In the next five to 10 years, half of our broadband communication could come from space, data centers could be in space; […] and if this is the case, we need massive rockets and cadence.”

That cadence will rely on reusability, which TEC plans to reach by using the same technology as SpaceX and Stoke: full-flow stage combustion “It’s the most difficult, but also the most efficient engine cycle in the world. It is the first time ever in Europe that a company develops such a rocket engine,” Huby said.

TEC’s advances haven’t gone unnoticed in Europe, with French president Macron and the European Commission’s president Ursula von der Leyen both praising its Series C. It is also not a coincidence that it was disclosed on the eve of the International Space Summit in Paris, where Huby hinted that related announcements will be made.

title: HomeKit Weekly: ULTRALOQ’s Bolt Fingerprint has everything you’d want except Home Key
snippet: My door has had a smart lock on it for 5-6 years, and I’ve tried plenty of options. The ULTRALOQ Bolt Fingerprint is a great option for almost anyone thanks to its Apple Home integration, built-in Wi-Fi, and plenty of ways to lock and unlock your door. Whether you’re looking for fingerprint ID unlock or a simple PIN, this lock has almost everything. more…
fullText:
My door has had a smart lock on it for 5-6 years, and I’ve tried plenty of options. The ULTRALOQ Bolt Fingerprint is a great option for almost anyone thanks to its Apple Home integration, built-in Wi-Fi, and plenty of ways to lock and unlock your door. Whether you’re looking for fingerprint ID unlock or a simple PIN, this lock has almost everything.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Apple Home support, but no Home Key

ULTRALOQ calls the Bolt Fingerprint its first smart lock fully integrated into Apple Home, and that integration is the major selling point for me. To be honest, I still miss Touch ID on my iPhone. You can lock and unlock the door from the Home app or with Siri, and if you have a HomePod or Apple TV as a hub, it works in automations and remote control just like any other Apple Home accessory with scene and automation support. 

That said, there’s one feature still missing for me: Home Key support. The ability to simply tap your iPhone or Apple Watch to unlock the door would take this lock to the next level. It’s literally the only thing missing, but it’s not a dealbreaker.

I hope ULTRALOQ considers adding this in a future model, because with Home Key, this lock could go from great to nearly perfect. The lock also works with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, SmartThings, and IFTTT, so you have flexibility regardless of your preferred smart home platform or what it might change to down the road. It runs on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi rather than Bluetooth, so you don’t need a separate bridge for basic remote control via their app. 

More ways to get in than you will ever need

The Bolt Fingerprint is not shy about unlock options, either. The fingerprint ID stores up to 50 fingers and up to 50 passcodes, app unlock from your phone, auto-unlock when you walk up to the door, and voice unlock through Siri, Alexa, or Google Assistant. Two physical keys are included as well, so you’re never fully locked out if the batteries are dead, etc. Not having physical keys is a non-starter for me.

You can also create up to 50 custom passcodes and hand out one-time or scheduled codes to friends, guests, cleaners, etc. If you rent out a house, this alone makes it worth a look.

There’s also a Lockout Mode that temporarily disables every electronic unlock method, including passcodes and app access, for anyone heading out of town who wants an extra layer of security while the house sits empty. I hadn’t considered this a feature in a smart lock, but it’s not a bad one to have.

Installation and adding to Apple Home

I’ve installed enough smart deadbolts over the past few years to know what I’m doing at this point. I can do it in around ten minutes, assuming I have my tools handy. There is no wiring or drilling required, assuming you are replacing a modern deadbolt. All you need is a Phillips head screwdriver, and you’ll also need to replace the strike plate on your door.

Once the lock is scanned into your Apple Home environment and assigned to a room, you can control it from the Home app, or add it to automations and scenes so multiple actions trigger together, as your lights turn on the moment the door unlocks, etc.

Wrap up on ULTRALOQ Bolt Fingerprint

Overall, the ULTRALOQ Bolt Fingerprint is a great choice for anyone who doesn’t require Home Key support. The fingerprint unlock is likely to become your go-to option for day-to-day use. Installation is easy. I’ve been using it on my office door for a while now, as I often have laptops waiting to be deployed in boxes that I want additional security for. I love how it unlocks as I get closer, and I love the logistics of tracking who has come and gone. The fingerprint support reminds me of the good old Touch ID days. 

You can buy the ULTRALOQ Bolt Fingerprint from Amazon or directly from ULTRALOQ.

title: Hypershell’s Halo Full-Leg Exoskeleton Made Me Dream Big About the Hikes I Hope to One Day Attempt
snippet: I forgot all about my creaky knees while trying out the all-terrain exoskeleton at IFA 2026.
fullText:
Do you consider yourself fit and healthy? I strength train, run, hike, climb and swim — albeit not according to any kind of training plan or schedule — and yet there are so many ways my body struggles on a daily basis. 

Even people who consider themselves to have a high level of cardiovascular fitness might lack strength, balance or flexibility. It’s almost impossible for one person to adhere to a truly holistic training plan. We all have weaknesses. We all know what it’s like to feel fatigued.

What if technology could pick up the slack? That’s the premise behind the Hypershell Halo, a full-leg exoskeleton unveiled at IFA in Berlin last week. This is far from the first Hypershell exoskeleton, but unlike previous models, the Halo extends further down the leg to provide support through the knee and calf, as well as through the thigh and hip.

The Hypershell Halo is flexible enough to allow a full range of movement.Katie Collins/CNET

The Hypershell unified architecture is one carbon-fiber, load-bearing structure with what the company is calling a “fish-spine adaptive joint” to allow for flexibility through the hip and into the leg. Its four-motor system is designed to power you through a whole range of movements while reducing knee-muscle fatigue by up to 40% across all types of terrain.

As someone with chronically creaky knees, I was excited to try the Hypershell Halo over the weekend at IFA. The target audience for an exoskeleton may be older adults and people with limited mobility, but Hypershell seems to be hoping the Halo will have broader appeal. Someone like me, who is active and enthusiastic about exploring the outdoors, but who sometimes reaches their physical limits earlier than they’d like, is also a contender.

I quickly discovered that putting the Hypershell Halo on is all part of the adventure. One belt attaches around the waist, and two flexible straps feed around the thighs. It takes a good few minutes and help from two people to adjust the exoskeleton to fit my proportions, but once the settings are right, it’s very quick to take on and off. (In an on-stage demonstration during the Halo launch event, I watched as the presenter put the exoskeleton on in just 16 seconds.)

My first impression is that I feel a little stiff and restricted, but that sensation immediately evaporates once I start moving. The kit weighs 2.6kg in total, with the majority of that distributed around my waist. I thought the Halo would take some getting used to and might disrupt my natural gait, but it doesn’t at all. Instead, I instantly feel lighter in my natural movements. Squatting and standing from a low seated position without using my hands for support and thrust is totally effortless. 

Most of the weight is distributed around your waist.Katie Collins/CNET

As I trample cheerfully all over Hypershell’s multistory booth, I find that that the only pressure anywhere in my legs is in my ankle joints. Going downstairs, I feel none of the usual pressure in my knees, thanks to the cushioning effect. The exoskeleton isn’t doing the work of walking for me, but it feels as though I could keep going for much longer.

This is one of the main use cases Hypershell is putting forward. Avid runners and hikers could potentially do far more than they’re used to without tiring. The Halo supports speeds of up to 17km per hour, which is a 2.5-hour marathon pace. Given that that’s the same as my half-marathon pace, I’d be interested to see what I could achieve while running in the Halo. 

As I descend the stairs, thinking about how difficult it usually is walking down the side of a mountain — just one long exercise in trying not to fall — I wonder whether the Halo could allow me to attempt some of the more challenging and vertiginous hikes I’m drawn to, but currently find too intimidating. I have my eye on a multiday Iceland trek, some steep summits in Lofoten and a whole bunch of routes in Patagonia. It also occurs to me that the Halo could be useful for groups with uneven levels of fitness or walking speeds. Could it be responsible for helping couples dodge the infamous alpine divorce? Or is that just delaying the inevitable?

For longer hikes, the battery supports up to 20 hours of use and can be easily swapped out. It only 370g, meaning it shouldn’t be too much of a burden to carry a spare or two.

I briefly switch the Halo to fitness mode, which increases the resistance for people who enjoy the feeling of physically working harder. I get the logic behind it, but I’m not one of these people I ask for it to be turned off again almost immediately. I guess it’s good that it exists for those who want it, but it’s not what I need after multiple days at a trade show.

One of the most interesting aspects of the Halo is how it uses AI. Over 30 sensors continuously capture lower-body movement, feeding data into the on-board AI chip, which can predict how you’re going to move 200ms before you actually do. This predictive technology means the Halo is adapting in real time to your activity, supporting your every move as you make it.

It can’t tell that this is happening while I’m wearing the exoskeleton, but I also suspect that that means it’s working as it should. After all, AI is the kind of technology that’s largely invisible when it’s at its most effective.

Perhaps the only drawback of wearing the Hypershell Halo is that it’s not subtle, and exoskeletons are still rare enough that it will likely attract attention if you wear one in public. If that doesn’t deter you and you’re ready to embrace life as cyborg in the here and now, the Hypershell Halo is available for preorder immediately, priced at $2,299.

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the IFA conference were covered in part by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

title: BASF subsidiary sues Apple over alleged Face ID patent infringement
snippet: TrinamiX, a subsidiary of BASF, says Apple’s current implementation of Face ID is infringing on several of its patents. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
TrinamiX, a subsidiary of BASF, says Apple’s current implementation of Face ID is infringing on several of its patents. Here are the details.

trinamiX says Face ID infringes seven patents

As first spotted by Reuters, trinamiX says newer versions of Apple’s Face ID, used in iPhones and iPad Pro models, infringe on seven of its patents.

In the lawsuit, trinamiX describes itself as a BASF spin-off that “has grown from a startup into an operating company that designs, develops, and commercializes advanced sensing technologies, including biometric imaging, three-dimensional vision, and near-infrared spectroscopy solutions for consumer and industrial applications.”

The patents trinamiX alleges Apple is infringing cover technology that can detect human skin during facial authentication, addressing an issue that, according to the lawsuit, allowed researchers to bypass the original version of Face ID using specially constructed 3D masks.

TrinamiX says its technology works by projecting a pattern of light onto a face and analyzing how that light reflects back to determine properties of the surface. Combined with 3D depth information, the company says this can distinguish human skin from materials used in photographs, masks, and other attempts to spoof facial authentication systems.

The seven patents listed in the lawsuit belong to two families:

Optical skin detection for face unlock (US Patents no. 12,530,925; 12,288,421; 12,456,334; 12,361,760)

Detector for identifying at least one material property (US Patents no. 12,298,394; 12,332,352; 12,461,238)

The lawsuit lists the following Apple devices among the “Accused Products”:

iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Plus, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max

iPhone 16, iPhone 16e, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max

iPhone 17, iPhone 17e, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max

iPhone Air

11-inch iPad Pro (4th generation)

12.9-inch iPad Pro (6th generation)

11-inch iPad Pro M4 and M5

13-inch iPad Pro M4 and M5

TrinamiX also mentions unspecified “other infringing iPhone and iPad models,” although it is not immediately clear which products it refers to.

After presenting its case, trinamiX asks the court to find that Apple infringed its patents, block Apple from making, using, selling, offering for sale, or importing the accused products, and award the company damages and attorneys’ fees.

The company is requesting a jury trial in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas.

title: JMGO’s New Projectors Go Big on Brightness and Refresh Rate. I Had a Look at IFA 2026
snippet: The new Iris series has a 120Hz refresh rate and lots of lumens. Here’s how they look.
fullText:
At the IFA show in Berlin, projector manufacturer JMGO launched its new Iris line. While externally similar to the N3 Ultimate and other models of its gimbal projectors, inside is a new light engine with even greater brightness and the new headline-grabbing feature at the show: a 120Hz refresh rate while running at full 4K resolution.

A 120Hz refresh rate isn’t exactly new in projectors, and definitely not with TVs, but with projectors, that refresh has been historically limited to 1080p. Is this a big deal? Sort of. It’s an interesting technical feat for sure, and shows where projectors can grow. For most people, it’s not likely a huge deal. Yet, a new DLP chip and design like what’s in JMGO’s new projectors is definitely worth having a look at. So I did.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

All the refreshes fit to refresh 

I got a brief look at the new Iris projectors at IFA, and there are two models. The Iris Ultra Max has a stated 6,500 lumens, a fully motorized gimbal and a higher native contrast ratio compared to its sibling. The less expensive Iris Ultra has “just” 4,500 lumens and only manual adjustments for the gimbal. Both models have a 0.9-1.7:1 optical zoom as well as horizontal and vertical image shift (separate from the gimbal). They also have a dual iris system to help dial in brightness and improve the dynamic contrast ratio.

I didn’t have any of my test gear with me, and no trade show is an ideal place to judge a product anyway, but the projectors certainly looked bright. JMGO had a side-by-side demo set up running fast-moving and fast-panning 60-frames-per-second content. One projector was running at a refresh rate of 60Hz, the other at 120Hz. The latter did have less blur on some aspects of the image. However, if you’re not watching 60fps content like sports or video games, I’d expect some severe motion-smoothing issues, aka the soap opera effect (this will be the case with any of these higher-refresh projectors). Then again, 120Hz is an even multiple of 24, so theoretically they could dejudder without interpolating frames. We’ll see.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

DLP has never had a significant issue with motion blur, so a faster refresh isn’t as big an improvement as it would be with, say, LCD. Reducing LCD motion blur is actually why we have faster refresh rates in TVs to begin with. JMGO says the faster refresh rate can also further minimize DLP’s infamous rainbow effect, where some people notice rainbow trails to certain objects on screen (or when they move their eyes). That could be very helpful for those susceptible to that issue.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

I really liked the N3 Ultimate when I reviewed it. It was, at that point anyway, the best gimbal projector. I’m not fully convinced of the need for a fully gimbaled projector for most people. But, with image shift and optical zoom, the N3 can fit in a lot of rooms regardless of how much or little you interact with the gimbal mechanism. And regardless of all that, its performance was excellent. If JMGO can keep the image quality just as high with these new projectors while increasing the already impressive brightness, that will be a very interesting projector. I’ll be getting one to test soon, especially to see if this whole 120Hz thing is worth the hype.

JMGO is expecting the MSRP of the Ultimate Max to be $3,699 and $2,299 for the Ultimate. Both start shipping in mid-October.
excerpt:
At the IFA show in Berlin, projector manufacturer JMGO launched its new Iris line. While externally similar to the N3 Ultimate and other models of its gimbal projectors, inside is a new light engine with even greater brightness and the new headline-grabbing feature at the show: a 120Hz refresh rate while running at full 4K resolution.

A 120Hz refresh rate isn’t exactly new in projectors, and definitely not with TVs, but with projectors, that refresh has been historically limited to 1080p. Is this a big deal? Sort of. It’s an interesting technical feat for sure, and shows where projectors can grow. For most people, it’s not likely a huge deal. Yet, a new DLP chip and design like what’s in JMGO’s new projectors is definitely worth having a look at. So I did.

title: Dyson’s First-Ever Dryer Brush, the Airsmooth, Is Now Available
snippet: Dyson’s new hair tools were designed to provide sleek locks without frizz or heat damage.
fullText:
At the Dyson Unveiled event at IFA 2026 in Berlin, Dyson announced a whopping 10 new products, including its first toothbrush, three robot vacuums, three air purifiers, a wet floor cleaner and two hair tools: its first dryer brush and a hair straightener designed to lessen heat damage. If you’re on the lookout for the latest tech for lustrous locks, here’s everything you need to know.

Dyson has round brush attachments for its Airwrap multistyler, but according to a press release, the Airsmooth is the brand’s first dedicated dryer brush. Designed for all hair types, it uses two different bristle types: PivotFlex bristles that bend up to 90 degrees and anti-snag bristles that collapse to release strands. Both were created to reduce uncomfortable hair-pulling. The PivotFlex bristles also have an open base that helps control and diffuse airflow, minimizing frizz.

A close-up of the Dyson Airsmooth’s bristles.Tara Brown/CNET

To further protect the hair’s natural texture and prevent damage, Airsmooth’s intelligent heat control measures temperature 100 times per second. 

For those who want a dryer brush they can take with them on the go, the Airsmooth has universal voltage, making it a great hair tool for travel. 

The Airsmooth’s dual-bristle design was developed with scalp comfort in mind.Dyson/CNET

“For folks who just want a drying brush and don’t want to spend over $600 on the Airwrap and all its attachments, the Airsmooth seems like a great option,” said Nasha Addarich Martínez, who tests hair tools for CNET. “This is similar to Shark, which has the FlexStyle (an Airwrap competitor), but it sells a dryer brush separately, too.”

The Corrale CoolShine

The successor to the Corrale straightener, the Corrale CoolShine includes Dyson’s first-of-its-kind cooling attachment that uses pipes containing a specific amount of water. When heat is applied to the hair, these pipes draw excess heat away from your strands to cool them and prevent damage.

You can choose from four different temperatures on the Corrale CoolShine. Tara Brown/CNET

Just like the Corrale, the Corrale CoolShine has flexing plate technology that shapes around the hair to gather it. 

According to Dyson, all of this technology combined leaves your locks cooler to the touch, with results lasting up to 24 hours and with up to 154% more shine compared to untreated hair. 

The Corrale CoolShine uses heat-extracting pipes to minimize damage.Dyson/CNET

Availability and price

The Airsmooth dryer brush is $250 and now available in ceramic pink through Dyson and Ulta. For $300, it’s also being sold at Sephora, but is currently out of stock.

As for the Corrale CoolShine straightener, it’s $329 and available on Sept. 15.

title: Apple will quickly become a dominant player in folding phones – Counterpoint
snippet: Counterpoint Research has predicted that global foldable phone shipments will surpass 100 million units by the end of this year, with the iPhone Ultra playing a major role in this growth. fullText:
Counterpoint Research has predicted that global foldable phone shipments will surpass 100 million units by the end of this year, with the iPhone Ultra playing a major role in this growth. The firm says it expects Apple to take 25% of the entire market this year – and it may be the biggest player by the same time next year.

In timing unlikely to be coincidental, the Xiaomi 18 Fold, leaked last month, is officially launching in China the day before Apple’s event …

iPhone Ultra set to have a major impact

While folding smartphones get a lot of attention, Counterpoint says that they currently only account for about 2% of the total market. This is expected to change significantly in the next 12 months, with 24% growth expected this year and a further 37% next.

The report says the market will see new products from Samsung, Apple, Huawei, Motorola, Honor, Google, Vivo, Oppo, and Xiaomi. The firm says Apple will be entering the market with a bang.

Apple’s entry will likely make an immediate impact. Counterpoint forecasts up to 6 million foldable iPhone shipments in 2026, giving Apple a 25% share of the global market and the No. 2 position, behind Samsung at 38% and ahead of Huawei at 22%.

It will be significant for Apple to achieve this ranking so quickly after entering the category, particularly given the relatively short selling window expected this year […] A full year of Apple sales will be a major driver, with Apple shipments expected to more than double and its share set to reach 40%.

That would exceed Samsung’s current 38% share.

Xiaomi launches 18 Fold on eve of Apple event

Xiaomi, which has made a name for itself by cloning many Apple products, appears to be seeking to do the same with its 18 Fold. 

The upcoming model, which shares the book format of the iPhone Ultra, which was leaked toward the end of last month before being shown off at IFA, has now officially launched on the eve of Apple’s Surprise and Shine event.

snippet: Users who post status updates on WhatsApp can now publish longer music clips, with the length limit doubled to 30 seconds. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Users who post status updates on WhatsApp can now publish longer music clips, with the length limit doubled to 30 seconds. Here are the details.

WhatsApp status gets a 30-second music clip limit

WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is rolling out support for music clips up to 30 seconds long in status updates.

Status updates are WhatsApp’s equivalent to Instagram Stories, and previously, posts containing music were limited to 15 seconds.

Now, users can select up to 30 seconds of a song to publish alongside a photo or share a music clip directly as a status update.

Here’s WABetaInfo on how to choose the music clip duration under the new 30-second limit:

After selecting a song from the music catalog, users can now see a clip duration picker in the music editor. The picker shows multiple options, up to 30 seconds. In this screen, users can scroll through them to select how many seconds of the song they want to include in the status. Although the maximum duration is 30 seconds, users can also choose a shorter clip if they prefer. Once they choose its duration, WhatsApp adds the music to the status update.

As is usually the case with WhatsApp’s server-side rollouts of new features, the new 30-second limit is still not available to everyone. However, WABetaInfo notes that some users on both iOS and Android are already seeing the new length limit. On iOS, the site lists WhatsApp version 26.35.72 as a compatible update.

title: New iPhone 18 Pro report details flagship camera feature and more
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be unveiled next week, and a new report offers fresh details on the flagship “mechanical aperture” camera feature that’s coming, plus mentions an improved vapor chamber and more. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be unveiled next week, and a new report offers fresh details on the flagship “mechanical aperture” camera feature that’s coming, plus mentions an improved vapor chamber and more.

Here’s what’s coming with iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, per Mark Gurman

Today Mark Gurman at Bloomberg published his latest expectations for the new iPhones being introduced on September 9.

While most of the report covers features reported previously, a few noteworthy details stand out.

For example, Apple has a new “mechanical aperture” camera feature coming to iPhone 18 Pro Max—and possibly the smaller iPhone 18 Pro too.

Despite plenty of reporting on this camera upgrade, which has also been called “variable aperture,” there have been minimal details on what it will enable. But Gurman reports today that it will be “for fine-tuning light adjustments and depth control.”

Additionally, the new report says iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will have “better battery life and improved vapor chambers to prevent overheating.”

Battery improvements were already expected, but good to see confirmed. The mention of improved vapor chambers is a new detail, though.

Apple first debuted a vapor chamber in the iPhone last year with iPhone 17 Pro. It seems the company already has a second-generation version ready to go.

Finally, Gurman says “in-house C2 modems” are coming to iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. While this isn’t a new rumor, it’s worth highlighting because some reports have claimed Apple is sticking with Qualcomm modems again this year.

For more on what to expect from iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, see our coverage here.

title: This Android phone has a detachable action camera, coming to the US for $999
snippet: IFA 2026 is delivering a pretty wild new Android phone that’s not only rugged, but has a GoPro-like action camera built-in which can be detached and used for capturing footage on the fly. more…
fullText:
IFA 2026 is delivering a pretty wild new Android phone that’s not only rugged, but has a GoPro-like action camera built-in which can be detached and used for capturing footage on the fly.

The RugOne XSnap 7 Pro first appeared earlier this year, but is now making a splash with official pricing and release information at IFA. The device is landing on Kickstarter next week and will cost $999 when it arrives in the US in October – €1,099 in Europe.

This rugged device comes from Ulephone, a known brand for these ruggedized Android smartphones, with “RugOne” being a new sub-brand under the company. And, as per usual, it’s a chonky device with a 19.1mm profile, IP68/IP69K/MIL-STD-810H certifications, and no need for a case with its rugged, drop-resistant design. It has a 6.67-inch FHD+ display using Gorilla Glass Victus on top, runs on a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 chip with 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, and has a massive 9,300 mAh battery. It even has a 64MP night vision camera to back up its 50MP main sensor. 

But the claim to fame here is a built-in, detachable action camera.

	

The camera attaches to the phone magnetically with a 133-degree field-of-view and 2.7K (1440p) recording. It can record for 40 minutes on its built-in battery and has 64GB of storage for up to eight hours of storage, but a built-in app on the phone can let the camera use the phone’s storage to offload that footage, and the phone also recharges the camera. The app can let you stream from the camera from up to 50 meters away and the action camera is waterproof up to 5 meters with no additional equipment.

It’s a wild idea, and one that actually seems more compelling than most of these rugged devices. A clear bit of utility, decent specs, and even a promise of software support – it XSnap 7 Pro ships with Android 16 and is promised updates through Android 20. 

What do you think?

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 has been fully restocked as trade-ins plummet; Fold 8 Ultra drops to $1,799
snippet: Samsung has fully restocked its smash-hit Galaxy Z Fold 8 while also discounting the usually-more-expensive Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra. more…
fullText:
Samsung has fully restocked its smash-hit Galaxy Z Fold 8 while also discounting the usually-more-expensive Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra.

Following some early stock shortages and a behind-the-scenes scramble to make more units, Samsung has fully restocked the Galaxy Z Fold 8 in the US. The wider foldable is currently available across every color and storage variant on Samsung.com, something that wasn’t the case even a couple of days ago. All variants are also shipping in two weeks or less, with most reporting shipping dates as early as next Tuesday.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 at Samsung.com

Samsung has dropped trade-in offers by a fair bit, now capping trade-in credits at $800 compared to $1,200 during the pre-order window, but it’s still not all that hard to get a good deal on a Fold 8.

Even more so the Fold 8 Ultra, which Samsung has officially discounted across all channels. Samsung.com, Best Buy, Amazon, and more have all cut the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s starting price from the usual $2,099 down to $1,799, a clear signal that the company’s former form factor isn’t resonating as much this year. The steep discount also makes the Ultra device cheaper than the wide Galaxy Z Fold 8. 

	

While Samsung shows the lower price on its main dashboard, it’s not showing for all users. There is a $350 instant savings credit available if you skip a trade-in, though, which cuts the price to $1,749. Galaxy Z Flip 8 is also down to $1,049 right now.

title: Hands-on: Orbitkey elevated its time-tested key organizer with a built-in Google Find Hub tracker
snippet: If you happen to walk past the Orbitkey’s setup at IFA in Berlin, you might have seen what the company is known for — key organizers. You’d be forgiven for not thinking these new key organizers had Google Find Hub trackers built in. more…
fullText:
If you happen to walk past the Orbitkey’s setup at IFA in Berlin, you might have seen what the company is known for — key organizers. You’d be forgiven for not thinking these new key organizers had Google Find Hub trackers built in.

Orbitkey isn’t new to Google Find Hub trackers, and certainly not key organizers. But its brand-new Key Organizer Tracker is the culmination of both, blending the visual design of what makes the company’s popular key holders so popular with more utility. I spent some time during IFA with the new key tool, and it’s already part of my EDC going forward.

The Key Organizer Tracker works with both Google Find Hub and Apple Find My networks by keeping a built-in tracker tucked in one of the sides. It looks thick at first glance, but I found that the new tracker/organizer is no thicker than some key-keepers, like the Ridge version I was lugging around. If your key organizer has a belt clip, Orbitkey’s Key Organizer Tracker will take up just as much space.

I’ve been using it for a few days during my IFA trip, and even though I don’t need to pull out my keys while on the go, I’ve toyed around with it enough to appreciate the design. Keys stay tucked and don’t spin, and the post has a semi-locking mechanism that prevents the keeper from loosening unnecessarily. Instead of a piece of spring steel sticking out to keep friction on your keys, Orbitkey uses a patented pressure ring that provides the perfect amount of pushback to keep them from spinning or locking in place.

	

Even the bottom key ring made for accompanying car keys is designed well. It’s fixed at the bottom, where the leather and plastic bend around. It doesn’t slide up into the space where keys sit, which makes pulling it out and grabbing the right key easier.

The tracker itself is no-nonsense, which is perfect. There’s a button for pairing and an LED to indicate status. It has a speaker to play loud chirps through the Google Find Hub app, and it charges via a magnetic pin charger included with the organizer. Orbitkey says the new Key Organizer Tracker lasts for 3-5 months, depending on your use. With how easy it is to charge, even with keys on it, that’s a respectable length of time.

Fit and finish feel great, as well. It has a faux-leather outer layer in tons of color options, and the rest of the keyboard’s build is made of sturdy, quality plastic.

Orbitkey also announced a new standalone tracker to complement the key holder. It’s shaped like a small popsicle stick, so it might not fit in your AirTag-branded accessories. Still, I’ve found it sort of slips into just about any bag. In Orbitkey’s new tech pouches, it fits into a dedicated pocket, so it won’t get lost in the clutter.

It has the same specs as the key tracker, with 3-5 months of battery and the same charging method.

Both the Orbitkey Key Organizer Tracker and the standalone Tracker come in a bunch of colors. Even though my pictures only show the black colorway, the rest of the company’s color options are vibrant. The key organizer comes in Black, Blush, Cobalt, Citrus, and Orange leather-free options. Leather versions come in Black, Tan, and Forest.

The Orbitkey Key Organizer Tracker starts at $69.90, and the Universal Tracker starts at $34.90. Both are on sale now, and the Key Organizer Tracker is currently available for pre-order.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 display corners can bend inward on purpose, Samsung says [Gallery]
snippet: The internet is mad. Shocking statement, I know, but this time it’s about a perceived quality control issue on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 that sees the display corners able to bend or flex inward, but that Samsung says is part of the design. more…
fullText:
The internet is mad. Shocking statement, I know, but this time it’s about a perceived quality control issue on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 that sees the display corners able to bend or flex inward, but that Samsung says is part of the design.

On Reddit, Samsung’s forums, and endless social media posts – as well as a heaping pile of clickbaity headlines – a “flaw” with the Fold 8 is being criticized. Some have noticed that when you apply pressure to the corner of the inner display on Samsung’s new foldable, the corner flexes inward, leaving a small gap between the display and the bezel until the pressure is released. It seems to be more pronounced on some devices rather than others – on my personal Fold 8, it’s barely noticeable.

Reactions have varied, with one thread calling on Samsung to recall the device due to this.

Via @TheGalox_
Via Samsung forums

Samsung says, though, that this is normal behavior.

	

In a statement to Business Post as well as a reply apparently through its forums, Samsung explains that the corners of the display flex to protect the display in the case that something is trapped within the folded display, as well as to “reduce the impact of interference or pressure between internal components of the display.” The statement explains:

If something like sand adheres to the top surface of the internal display, the screen could get scratched when the Fold is folded. We designed it so the display indents slightly to provide a cushioning effect and prevent damage. Since this feature was prepared to ensure consumers do not experience inconvenience, we have not provided a separate official explanation.

One of the main concerns here was in regards to water resistance, with many assuming that this gap would let water get into the internals of the device. This was tested directly by one user, who applied pressure to the display corners while the Fold 8 was entirely submerged in water, with the foldable coming out unscathed. 

What do you think?

title: Samsung ‘advice’ to Apple suggests it fears the build quality of the iPhone Duo
snippet: Samsung says it welcomes Apple’s entry into the foldable smartphone market, although the company appears to feel threatened by the likely build quality of the iPhone Duo/Ultra. A Samsung exec said he sees Apple’s launch as “acknowledging and recognizing” the Korean company’s “pioneering” lead … more…
fullText:
Samsung says it welcomes Apple’s entry into the foldable smartphone market, although the company appears to feel threatened by the likely build quality of the iPhone Duo/Ultra.

A Samsung exec said he sees Apple’s launch as “acknowledging and recognizing” the Korean company’s “pioneering” lead …

Samsung currently dominates the folding smartphone market, but a report yesterday suggests that’s likely to change within the next twelve months. A leading market intelligence company predicted that Apple will own 40% of the market by this time next year; Samsung currently has a 38% share.

Hee-Cheul Moon, one of Samsung’s R&D leads, spoke to Wired.

On the eve of Apple’s highly anticipated folding iPhone, Samsung […] says the competition is “absolutely welcome” […]

“Seeing these other brands entering the market, we feel very proud of ourselves that the value that we pioneered with this new category of foldables is being acknowledged and recognized,” Moon says.

Samsung has suffered major problems with the build quality of its foldables, while Apple is believed to have waited so long precisely because it wanted to ensure it could overcome the quality issues that have plagued competing devices. Specifically, Apple wanted to ensure the crease was almost invisible when unfolded, and that the device would be robust enough to withstand constant folding and unfolding without issue.

Apple reportedly put a huge amount of engineering work into the quality of the hinge, and its robustness seems likely to carry a weight penalty – and it’s this which Samsung is seizing upon as an implied criticism.

Moon said, “The key to providing the highest customer value in this market is all about the weight of the device. As you know, it’s not easy.”

Wired reports that Apple’s foldable is expected to weigh around 235g, while Samsung’s Galaxy Fold 8 weighs 201g.

fullText:
As the debut of Googlebook quietly approaches, a week full of new laptop launches at IFA continues to make me wonder why literally anyone should be even a tiny bit interested in Google’s new platform.

This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!

Googlebook made its debut earlier this year as the company’s Android-based desktop platform that will replace ChromeOS and, frankly, I’ve spent the last couple of months just sitting here stewing over the complete lack of information on what this platform is supposed to do and why anyone should care. Truly, I cannot remember the last time I was this skeptical about a Google product – is this how other people felt about Stadia?

At this point, not much has changed.

	

We’ve seen leaks of some of the first Googlebook laptops from Asus and Lenovo, while Acer was spotted teasing its Googlebook at IFA in Berlin. Some early apps have shown up too, including “Magic Pointer” which is the one new feature Google has actually shown off from this platform, a “Desktop Camera” app, and “Look up” which is in fact not a reference to that DiCaprio movie but instead an AI-powered experience that lets you interact with text to find relevant information such as definitions, flight tracking, and more. That one works on some Android phones, too. 

Yet, I still cannot fathom where Googlebooks fit into the larger market. ChromeOS had a clear selling point – stable and usable software on low-cost hardware, with later generations adding in some clever AI features and using more capable hardware. But where Googlebook might have been interesting from a cost perspective, a focus on “premium” hardware combined with RAMageddon and a sea of MacBook Neo competitors… I just don’t get it folks. 

The new IdeaPad Vibe from Lenovo and the Dell 14S were both announced this week as direct answers to Apple’s hit budget-conscious laptop, and Google is literally going in the opposite direction.

Damien laid out some potential ideas back in June, such as a focus on AI-aided vibe coding, but it’s still hard to imagine Google’s pitch at this point. Windows laptops are getting more affordable in the wake of the MacBook Neo, and is anyone looking to spend money on tech they don’t need to right now? Maybe I’m just having trouble seeing the potential or the positives here, but I can’t remember the last time I was so sour on a potential new Google launch. 

What do you think?

title: Apple has reportedly canceled innovative product that was ‘Ternus priority’
snippet: A new Omdia research note today outlined Apple’s reported Mac and iPad roadmap for the years ahead, and it also mentioned that a key rumored product has been canceled. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new Omdia research note today outlined Apple’s reported Mac and iPad roadmap for the years ahead, and it also mentioned that a key rumored product has been canceled. Here are the details.

Foldable iPad/Mac hybrid that was John Ternus ‘priority’ has reportedly been canceled

For years, rumors have suggested that the iPhone will be just the first Apple product line to adopt foldable displays.

Reporting suggests that a larger, roughly 18- or 20-inch foldable iPad/Mac hybrid device has been in the works for years. At one point it was believed to be coming as early as 2026 before later being pushed to 2028.

Earlier this year, Mark Gurman called the product a “Ternus priority” but also suggested it may never launch. He wrote:

Apple has been working on a roughly 20-inch foldable iPad. This device has been a Ternus priority but may end up being a wacky experiment that doesn’t see the light of day, according to several people who have worked on it.

You can find a good overview of prior rumors about the product here.

According to today’s Omdia report, it seems Gurman’s suspicions may have been right. It says: “product plans for 16.1-inch to 18-inch foldable MacBooks have been canceled.”

Based on prior rumors, this seems to be the same product previously covered by Gurman and others.

	

It’s very possible Apple is taking a “wait and see” approach with this foldable product as it gauges reception to the foldable iPhone Ultra. If iPhone Ultra is a hit, maybe the company will accelerate development of the iPad/MacBook hybrid.

But perhaps with the current memory crisis causing product pricing to rise so significantly already, Apple doesn’t see a current path forward for an ultra-premium, innovative foldable device like this.

What do you think of the rumored foldable iPad/MacBook being canceled? Let us know in the comments.

Update 9/7:

Still rolling out (beta)

These are Messages features that Google announced or have been spotted in the wild by beta users.

Customizable attachments grid

Google is testing two designs, with the one on the right taking up more of your screen.

	

Learn more

Instead of a top toolbar, long-pressing on a message or image opens a floating menu as the background blurs. Another press lets you copy just a part of the chat. Previously, you had to copy the entire message.

Learn more

iOS 27 adds replies & photo reactions to Android-iPhone RCS

When iOS 27 launches this fall, Android-iPhone conversations over RCS will gain support for inline replies that include quotes, as well as photo reactions with the actual emoji instead of just the text description. This feature is currently in beta.

More

Read receipts redesign II

In recent weeks, Google Messages has mostly reverted to the two-circle read receipts underneath the message design after trying a single circle within the bubble.

Google is now testing a variant that uses the old icons but moves the timestamp and encryption lock. You now view that information by swiping left, with direct replies accessed by a right swipe.

Learn more

Messages for web removing QR code pairing

Going forward, Messages for web users will have to use Google Account sign-in. As of late April, the QR code method is still available.

Learn more

Read receipts redesign I

Read receipts are now placed in a circle at the bottom-right corner of message bubbles and images. You swipe left to see timestamps and the encryption lock, while you can swipe right to reply. This first started appearing in August of 2024, but is now seeing wide beta and stable availability.

[Rolling out] Google Keep in Google Messages

The new Google Keep integration lets you quickly create and share notes inside chats. If you don’t see a contextual suggestion to “Create list,” open the ‘plus’ menu for a new “Keep Notes” tile.

This will slide up a sheet that shows your list of notes and the “Create a note” button. Upon selecting or starting a note, you’ll see a send button in the bottom-right corner. Afterward, there’s a live preview in the conversation thread.

As of early September, Google Messages is still rolling out the Keep integration.

Chat theme

Google Messages now lets you extensively customize conversations with a “Chat theme.” Replacing “Change colors” from 2024, you access this new option from the three-dot overflow menu. Be on the lookout for a red badge when this is rolled out for your phone. Themes will only appear on your device.

The Colors carousel themes message bubbles. There are nine options, with Dynamic Color being the first option and responding to the background of your chat.

	

The Wallpapers option lets you change the background of the conversation. In addition to uploading your own image, Google provides the following collections: Animals, Architecture, Black & White, Cityscapes, Landscapes, Macro, Space, Sunsets, and Textures.

title: Samsung is shutting down ‘Quick Measure’ and ‘AR Doodle’ apps for Galaxy phones
snippet: Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year. more…
fullText:
Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year.

Confirmed in Galaxy Store listings for both the “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” apps, Samsung will be shutting down these AR experiences on December 31, 2026. Samsung explains that both will be “returning with improved services in the future.”

“Quick Measure” is an AR app that lets you get measurements of real-world distance from your phone, while “AR Doodle” lets you “draw” on real-world locations through the camera app.

The shutdown will block new downloads of both apps, while also pulling the plug on any future updates. The app won’t just stop working immediately, but any OS updates will break the apps in time. Notably, Samsung seems to have hidden both app listings on the latest One UI versions, making them inivisible in the Galaxy Store.

	

Samsung says:

Please be advised that service for the Quick measure app is scheduled to be terminated on 31 December 2026.

After this date, new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it is already downloaded, but please be aware that some features may not function properly.

Additionally, compatibility support for the Quick measure app will no longer be provided for future OS updates.

We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause and thank all our customers for their loyal use of the Quick measure app. We are committed to returning with improved services in the future.

It’s unclear when these replacement apps might arrive, but it’s certainly a shame to see these going away.

title: Google Messages slowly rolling out fix for bug that randomly sends old texts to other people
snippet: A bug in Google Messages is causing the app to randomly send old text messages to other random people and, while it’s still happening, a fix is slowly on the way. more…
fullText:
A bug in Google Messages is causing the app to randomly send old text messages to other random people and, while it’s still happening, a fix is slowly on the way.

The issue at play here sees Google Messages reviving old messages that were sent to a contact and sending those alongside another new message to a different contact. You can see the problem, right? A message meant for your significant other could theoretically be sent to your parents, for example. It’s been reported by many users in recent weeks, with the problem even visible in real time; some have tested sending themselves messages only to see old messages randomly inserted into the same thread.

Highlighted by Droid-Life, there are still reports of this behavior popping up right now, with some reports popping up just in the past day.

It’s not happening for everyone, but it’s obviously a major issue for those affected. Sending old messages to random people could, at the very least, result in confusion, but could go as far as revealing private information. 

	

In a statement, Google confirmed that it is aware of the issue and has a fix, but it’s not rolling out quickly. Google said:

We’re currently rolling out a fix that will reach everyone over the coming weeks. Please ensure you stay up to date with the most recent version of Google Messages.

That was on September 2, and reports continue to pop up now, the better part of a week later. Updates continue to land on Google Play, so go check for a patch if you’re affected. Let us know in the comments below if you’re running into this bug.

title: Apple faces new UK rules over nude images on children’s iPhones
snippet: Bloomberg reports that the UK intends to introduce legislation that would require Apple and Google to “stop children from taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their phones and tablets.” Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that the UK intends to introduce legislation that would require Apple and Google to “stop children from taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their phones and tablets.” Here are the details.

Apple says it plans to strengthen Communication Safety

The UK’s Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said in a statement to Parliament today that the government plans to introduce new legislation requiring major tech platforms, including Apple and Google, to build “device-level protections” meant to prevent children from “taking, sharing, or viewing nude images on their devices.”

The move, which she says will be brought to Parliament “as soon as we can,” follows a three-month deadline given to tech companies in June to introduce such protections voluntarily.

In her speech to the House of Commons, Nandy acknowledged that Apple and Google have made “meaningful changes” since then, but said those changes “do not meet the scale of this crisis.”

From her statement:

Children are facing unacceptable levels of sexual harm online. They are being groomed, coerced, and manipulated into creating and sharing intimate images across online services.

The Internet Watch Foundation believes that 91% of these images are self-generated by children themselves. They are used for blackmail and sexual extortion.

Each year, around 9,000 child sexual abuse offences involve an online element, with under 18s the subject of almost a quarter of online blackmail.

Nandy added that device-level protections are just one of two measures the government plans to pursue, the second being requirements for apps used by children “to prevent them from accessing or sharing nudity”:

We will explore what legislation is needed to implement this commitment, with a view to moving as quickly as possible. This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.

In a statement to Bloomberg, Apple said that it shares “the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”

Apple also said that it introduced in 2021, “a feature that prevents children from viewing or sharing photos or videos that contain nudity,” adding that “it now includes support for third-party apps.”
