title: Leaker claims iPhone 18 Pro chip will have 7 GPU cores and faster RAM
snippet: A Chinese leaker with some track record has posted images of claimed circuit diagrams of the upcoming iPhone 18 Pro models. These suggest that the new A20 Pro chip may have seven GPU cores – one more than its predecessor – and a faster memory interface … more…
fullText:
A Chinese leaker with some track record has posted images of claimed circuit diagrams of the upcoming iPhone 18 Pro models.

These suggest that the new A20 Pro chip may have seven GPU cores – one more than its predecessor – and a faster memory interface … 

The images posted by Weibo user Fried White Rice are not of the A20 Pro chip itself, but rather diagrams of where the chip will be attached to the underlying circuit board. From this, they’re making inferences about the power and architecture of the new chip, drawing two main conclusions about likely improvements.

First, the diagrams point to six CPU cores in the same configuration as last year’s model: two high-performance ones and four efficiency cores. However, it appears that the cache memory for the efficiency cores has been increased.

We can see that the L2 cache for the small CPU cores has been increased—likely from 6 MB in the A19 Pro to 8 MB—while the L2 cache for the big CPU cores remains unchanged at 16 MB.

Trying to determine the number of GPU cores from the limited information provided by the solder diagrams is tricky, with six, seven and eight cores all possibilities. However, they conclude that seven cores is the most likely.

Again relying on the overall outline and solder‑ball positions, we can roughly deduce the GPU’s layout and explore several dozen configurations across three core counts—6, 7, and 8 cores. Ultimately, the 7‑core GPU configuration emerges as the most plausible arrangement.

Fixed Focus Digital recently suggested that the A20 Pro chip will be 18% faster than its predecessor with 30% better power efficiency.

9to5Mac’s Take

The Weibo account does have a certain amount of credibility, but this kind of indirect inference is very much a dark art. While the conclusions drawn are indeed plausible, they shouldn’t be viewed as anything more than informed guesses.

title: Nintendo Reveals Ocarina of Time Remake Release Date, a Zelda Switch 2 and a Real Ocarina
snippet: Nintendo is marking four decades of Zelda with special hardware, playable ocarinas and more ways for fans to celebrate the legendary series.
fullText:
Nintendo held its The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct on Tuesday to reveal a new release for one of its biggest franchises. The big news was the reveal of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake release date or a special edition Nintendo Switch 2. But the gaming giant also announced an actual ocarina that fans can buy to annoy their friends and family while learning how to play.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake will launch on Nov. 5, according to Tuesday’s presentation. A week before its release, a special edition Switch 2 for the 40th anniversary will be released on Oct. 29, along with a Switch 2 Pro Controller and carrying case. Then, to complete the anniversary package for Zelda fans, Nintendo plans to release an official ocarina identical to the one Link plays throughout Ocarina of Time. There will be a traditional acoustic model and an electric version made by Hori.

The main star of Tuesday’s direct was the Ocarina of Time remake. As expected, it will make full use of the Switch 2’s graphics power to give a modern look to the almost 30-year-old game, first released for the N64. Visuals weren’t the only upgrades, as controlling Link is much easier using both analog sticks, which weren’t around in 1998, and instead of jumping automatically near any ledge, there’s a jump button to let Link get across gaps.

Another interesting feature involves the ocarina Link uses in the game. This is a key item as it lets Link do various magical feats when a certain tune is played by pressing the correct buttons. Something different is that players can now hum the tune, and the game will recognize the sound via the Switch 2’s microphone and complete the input to activate the song.

Only the intro sequence of the game in Kokiri Forest and the first section of Hyrule Castle Town were shown during the presentation. All the characters received a visual upgrade as well as voices, with new fully voiced cutscenes. Link, however, is still not going to talk. 

First-time players who get lost or a little confused in the game will be able to check out Zelda Notes, a new feature added into the Nintendo Switch app that lets players track their progress, gives some hints on in-game location and provides other info for players.

Before playing Ocarina of Time remake, fans can pick up the Nintendo Switch 2: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition system. The new Switch 2 variant will have a unique look on the console and dock inspired by the game. There will also be a Switch 2 Pro Controller and a carrying case with their own inspired looks that will be sold separately. Nintendo also plans to have an exclusive Switch 2 Pro Controller with its own display stand for sale only at the Nintendo Store in New York City and San Francisco.

Nintendo

Then, there’s the ocarina. Two ocarinas will be available for purchase: a standard acoustic ocarina and an electric one made by Hori that can play songs via a button. Eiji Aonuma, the producer of the Zelda series, gave a demo of how the ocarina sounds during the show. Nintendo didn’t provide a price or release date for these ocarinas, but it said in a press release that they will be available later this year.

Nintendo/Screenshot by CNET

Other Zelda news mentioned in the show was the April 30, 2027, release date for a film based on the game, officially called The Legend of Zelda. A 40th anniversary concert series featuring the game’s music will also kick off in January in Japan and in February in the US, starting in Chicago. Also out next year are the Young Link and Young Zelda amiibo figures.

Nintendo didn’t officially put a price on the Ocarina of Time remake, but the digital version is expected to be $60. There is a listing for the physical version of the game on the Nintendo Store for $70 that appeared shortly after the presentation and was taken down by Nintendo. It’s unclear what items shown during the event will be available at other retailers and which ones will be available only through the Nintendo Store.

title: Google Find Hub update brings new ‘Remembered’ tab with Gemini
snippet: Following last week’s Android Drop, Google is now rolling out an app update that brings the “Remembered” tab to Find Hub. more…
fullText:
Following last week’s Android Drop, Google is now rolling out an app update that brings the “Remembered” tab to Find Hub.

After updating, you’ll see a new tab join Devices and People. Remembered uses a bookmark icon badged by the Gemini spark. 

You can “Tell Gemini to remember where you put everyday belongings,” like: “Remember that I put my passport in my top dresser drawer.” The FAB (floating action button) has an “Ask Gemini” shortcut that opens the full app, while there’s also a “Manual entry” option.

It starts by giving the item a “Name” and “Storage spot.” You can add more details afterwards, including a picture, “Location” (like your Home), and any “Notes.” 

	

Find Hub lists everything you’ve stored in the sheet, with Gemini also having this information for hands-free interaction. 

Version 3.1.732-02 of Find Hub is rolling out now via the Google Play Store. It’s not yet widely available.

title: Xiaomi 18 Fold goes on sale with full specs and a Galaxy Z Fold 8 comparison [Gallery]
snippet: Following an appearance at IFA 2026 last week, Xiaomi has posted the full details of its new wide Fold, while it’s also been directly compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8. more…
fullText:
Following an appearance at IFA 2026 last week, Xiaomi has posted the full details of its new wide Fold, while it’s also been directly compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

Pre-orders for the Xiaomi 18 Fold are now open in China and, with that, a full breakdown of the foldable’s specs. This includes a 5.38-inch outer display, 7.58-inch inner display, as well as the Xiaomi XRing O3 chipset that was previously announced. But, going further down the list, there are some other powerful specs on offer.

A 6,000 mAh battery (with 67W wired charging/50W wireless) powers the show, way bigger than the 4,800 mAh battery in Samsung’s device. That’s despite a clear difference in size. As The Verge shows in a hands-on, Samsung’s wide foldable is both taller and narrower than Xiaomi’s when folded. The same article calls out that Xiaomi’s device has almost the exact aspect ratio as an IMAX display. 

Images via The Verge

Xiaomi’s listing further details the dimensions at 117.8 x 83.6 x 10.68mm when the foldable is closed, opening up to 163.8mm wide and 5.02mm thick when unfolded. Storage and memory options range from 12GB + 256GB up to 16GB + 1TB. 

	

The triple camera array around back includes a 200MP main sensor, 50MP 3.5x telephoto, and a 50MP ultrawide too. 

Colors include “Warm Gold,” “White,” “Black,” and “Nishino Red” (translated).

There’s also a light pink “Ceramic” model.

The Xiaomi 18 Fold is available for purchase now in China starting at ¥10,999. Directly converted, that’s just shy of $1,640 USD. It’s still unclear if or when this foldable might make its way to global markets, but it’s certainly an intriguing release.

title: Apple fixes frustrating TestFlight app regression that search feature update added
snippet: Back in July, Apple updated its TestFlight app with a basic search feature. While you might think this simple update would be universally welcomed, the same TestFlight app introduced a pretty frustrating bug for a lot of users. more…
fullText:
Back in July, Apple updated its TestFlight app with a basic search feature. While you might think this simple update would be universally welcomed, the same TestFlight app introduced a pretty frustrating bug for a lot of users.

Personally, I wasn’t affected by the bug in a way that I noticed. For this reason, I thought the TestFlight update was a simple but significant step forward.

Sometimes a small change can make a big impact. That’s especially true for Apple’s latest TestFlight update for users with a lot of pre-release software.

Apple just updated TestFlight for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more. The new version, 4.3, introduces “a search field to quickly find apps.” 

In retrospect, I did notice something odd that I flagged at the end of the post (but got backwards in my assessment):

The update also surfaced more apps in the “previously tested” category, so maybe the usual bug fix and performance improvements may relate to that.

I missed that this was actually the bug, I think, because I left several years of app TestFlights to “merge” my separate iCloud and App Store Apple accounts last year. Inconvenient requirement, but worth it for me.

Anyway, the TestFlight app bug didn’t go unnoticed by John Vorhees at MacStories:

So, you can imagine my excitement when I read a post by Zac Hall at 9to5Mac that a search field had been added to TestFlight. “Finally,” I thought to myself. I stopped what I was doing and updated the app immediately. […]

Unfortunately, this story comes with one very big “but.” Previously, TestFlight betas were listed in reverse chronological order, which I liked. […]

Well, those expired betas are now scattered among the active TestFlight betas in an alphabetical list and it seems that the expired beta list has been expanded to include every single beta I’ve ever been a part of. I did a rough count and for me that’s nearly 800 app listings. As you can imagine, the active betas in that list are few and far between. Search helps, but scrolling is no longer an option.

Then in August, John Gruber wrote an essay on Daring Fireball about the TestFlight update and bug:

I didn’t complain about this when the sort order changed last month because I figured it was an oopsie — that alphabetical order was supposed to kick in only when displaying search results, not by default. But here we are a month later and the presentation of apps in TestFlight makes me a little irritated every day. 

Last night, more than a month after the bug was introduced (and flagged by Vorhees), Apple has updated TestFlight for the first time. While the release notes only point to bug fixes, the update does indeed fix the bug in question. 

TestFlight version 4.3.1 is the fix for those experiencing the regression.

title: Google Home update restores support for older Chromecast streamers, Home Mini
snippet: A rogue Google Home update earlier this year partially broke support for some older Chromecast streamers and other devices, but the latest update has restored it. more…
fullText:
A rogue Google Home update earlier this year partially broke support for some older Chromecast streamers and other devices, but the latest update has restored it. 

If you’re still using one of the original Chromecast streaming dongles over a decade later, first of all, kudos to you. While Google has technically dropped software support for its original 2013 streamer, the company continues to provide updates and support for other models. 

Back in May, it seemed as though the end had come for that first-gen device as support faltered in the Home app, but a fix arrived later on. It didn’t take long for further issues to appear, though. There was another wave of reports in late July, affecting not only the first-gen Chromecast, but also the 2015 model and Google Home Mini. The issue was primarily affecting setup, but also functionality to some extent, and mostly on the Android version of the Google Home app.

Google says this should be fixed as of Google Home v4.26 which is available now.

	

In a comment shared across several Reddit threads, Google explains:

We’ve resolved an issue that was impacting the ability to set up some older Chromecast and Google Home devices. If you haven’t already, factory reset their speaker or update your Google Home app to version 4.26 and try again…

You can download Google Home v4.26 via the Play Store, but you likely already have it installed.

title: I Went Eyes-On With the Aurzen Zip Pro Foldable, Portable Projector. It’s Ready to Shine Your Entertainment Anywhere
snippet: It has the same fun, foldable design as Aurzen’s other Zip, but now it’s larger and far more capable.
fullText:
Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

A few months ago, I reviewed the Zip Cyber, a cyberpunk-themed pocket projector from Aurzen. It wasn’t very bright, but the trifold design made it extremely pocketable, and the overall appearance was great. 

At IFA, Aurzen debuted the Zip Pro, an updated and upgraded projector with 1080p resolution and twice the brightness. The exterior design is similar, keeping some aspects of the cyberpunk aesthetic (wise, in my opinion) and adding a small touchscreen on the top to aid setup. 

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

While still sporting what Aurzen calls “trifold” (there are two hinges), the Zip Pro is actually slightly larger than the Zip and Zip Cyber at 4.5 by 3.8 by 1.7 inches versus 3.3 by 3.1 by 1 inches. So, it’s nearly three times the total volume and about twice the weight. This is still a remarkably small projector, just less pocketable than the original. It would get swallowed by any backpack. 

Inside, there’s the aforementioned bump up to 1080p, as well as a slightly larger battery. Aurzen says it has 2.5 hours of playtime compared to the Zip’s 1.5 hours. Since it recharges via USB-C, though, you can extend playtime with any decent portable battery pack. So, with the improved performance, the larger size seems a reasonable trade-off. 

The Zip Cyber (top) and the Zip Pro were on display at IFA.Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

I got a quick look at the Zip Pro at IFA, and it did seem brighter, as evidenced by far larger image sizes to demo the projector compared to how I’ve seen it demo the Zip. The 200-lumen range makes the Pro far more usable in a wider variety of situations. It competes specs-wise,with the Anker Capsule 3, which was pricey but good. The Zip Pro is more expensive, but most tech is now compared to when the Capsule 3 was launched.

Connectivity

The biggest issue with the Zip Cyber was that it was a challenge to get anything onto it to watch. There’s still no HDMI, but it does have AirLink, Miracast, AirPlay P2P, DLNA and, especially notable since it was missing in the original Zip, Google Cast. You can also connect via USB-C to watch content from your phone.

title: Google Clock rolls out redesign of Timers with presets on Android
snippet: Following the new app icon, Google Clock has rolled out a redesigned Timers tab. This follows yesterday’s update to the Now Playing app. more…
fullText:
Following the new app icon, Google Clock has rolled out a redesigned Timers tab. This follows yesterday’s update to the Now Playing app.

The big change is that Google has introduced presets for 1, 5, 10, and 15 minutes that immediately start counting down once tapped. Google has tweaked the numbers at the top with Hours, Minutes, and Seconds replacing h, m, and s.

A big green “Start” pill replaces the previous icon at the bottom of the screen. Finally, the number pad no longer uses circular backgrounds. This tweak makes the screen feel flatter, with the interface now much busier but more efficient.

Old vs. new

	

If you have multiple timers, Google has shrunk down the cards and now offers a grid instead of the previous scrollable list. This is a much better use of screen real estate, while there are no changes to the single-timer look. The pause button is now inside the circular countdown, while reset is outside. 

This Timers redesign is rolling out as part of a server-side update with version 9.1 of Google Clock. If you’re not seeing it yet, Force stop from App info.

title: How to check if Motion Assist has rolled out to your Android 17 phone
snippet: Following the announcement on Tuesday, Google is slowly rolling out Motion Assist to phones running Android 17. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement on Tuesday, Google is slowly rolling out Motion Assist to phones running Android 17.

Once rolled out, you can search for “motion assist” in the Settings app. The long way is Settings app > Google > All services tab > Personal & device safety > Motion assist. Appearing alongside Advanced Protection and Theft protection, this new feature is part of Google Play services.

The preference menu lets you have Motion Assist automatically “Start in a moving vehicle,” but Google also recommends adding the Quick Settings Tile. This lets you manually enable and disable “from any screen.” You can add it from this page or the usual edit screen under “From system apps.” Once active, there’s also a system notification that lets you disable with a tap.

The Customize menu lets you adjust:

	

Color: Based on system, Red, Yellow, Green, Blue

Shape: Circle, Square, Pentagon, Diamond

Opacity: Slider

Randomization: “Color and shape change every few seconds”

The moving shapes adjust to the device’s motion and “may help reduce motion sickness when you’re in a moving vehicle.” On the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you get three columns of shapes on the left and right edges, while Google’s phone example shows two.

Motion Assist is not yet widely rolled out. We’re seeing it with version 26.33.32 of Google Play services, but there’s a server-side component. As of today, it’s only appearing on one of our devices.

title: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Two new display upgrades coming next week
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will have the same screen sizes as their predecessors, but rumors indicate their displays will be upgraded in two other ways. Here’s what’s coming. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will have the same screen sizes as their predecessors, but rumors indicate their displays will be upgraded in two other ways. Here’s what’s coming.

#1: LTPO+ technology

LTPO is the technology that has long powered the iPhone’s Always-On and ProMotion display features. And in iPhone 18 Pro, Apple is rumored to be moving to the more advanced LTPO+.

Per The Elec:

Conventional LTPO applies oxide materials to switching thin-film transistors (TFTs). LTPO+ extends oxide usage to driving TFTs as well, enabling finer current control for OLED light emission and allowing displays to optimize operation based on surrounding conditions and user environments, improving battery efficiency.

Benefits of LTPO+ include reduced screen flickering in low-light environments thanks to more responsive adjustments, plus improved power efficiency. Thus, iPhone 18 Pro users should enjoy even more consistent display performance at a lower battery cost.

#2: Reduced Dynamic Island cutout

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max’s displays are also expected to have a reduced Dynamic Island cutout. Thus, the useable screen space will expand slightly.

The new Dynamic Island is rumored to be about 35% smaller than what iPhone 17 Pro offers. This size is even hinted at already by iOS 27 in Siri’s new design.

Apple debuted the Dynamic Island on iPhone 14 Pro back in 2022. While software features related to the Dynamic Island and Live Activities have expanded over time, the physical cutout has remained unchanged.

With iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Apple is finally moving a step closer to the dream of a cutout-free display.

title: Annoyingly, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the best advert for an iPhone Fold yet
snippet: Samsung has beaten Apple to the punch, but I’m annoyed that while it’s, in fact, a fantastic device, it’ll only help bolster the sales of the long-rumored iPhone Fold. more…
fullText:
Samsung has beaten Apple to the punch, but I’m annoyed that while it’s, in fact, a fantastic device, it’ll only help bolster the sales of the long-rumored iPhone Fold.

It is a really ironic position for Samsung to find itself in. They have spent years flexing their engineering muscle, burning through iterations, and pushing folding display technology to its absolute limit to lead this space. Although I would argue that some others are doing the “traditional” foldable better now.

Yet despite all the leading, innovating, and market domination, Samsung’s latest flagship wide-body foldable might just end up courting buyers right into Apple’s hands with its iPhone Fold.

The cynic in me sort of feels that, like the Galaxy S25 Edge, getting ahead of Apple was a calculated play to try and court those who are intrigued by the form factor, but maybe not ready to commit to the very compromised 1:1 aspect-ratio’d Z Folds. It’s hard to argue that most folding phones are narrow devices that feel like holding a thick TV remote when closed.

	

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is refreshing compared to Samsung’s previous folding phones because it’s leaning into the entertainment strengths that are supposedly why folding phones are so popular. As with any tech product, there are always going to be compromises, especially when it’s a 2-in-1 experience. Foldables are mature, but the wide body feels like it’s ready to be fully explored. In my mind, a wide-body folding phone is the optimal design. The final form is the tri-fold, which, coincidentally, Samsung has managed to ship to those with deep enough pockets.

Back to the Fold 8: for the most part, many reviews have pointed out how refreshing the Z Fold 8 is despite the fact that Oppo and Google did it first. Samsung has just done it better than anyone thus far. In fact, the Z Fold 8 is easily one of my favorite smartphones of the last few years. As soon as I picked it up, it made sense. I carry it as a secondary phone with a backup SIM. It is my Balatro-playing, web-scrolling, book-reading, movie-watching phone. It’s a small tablet, but also a small phone; there’s literally nothing to hate in my mind.

It probably doesn’t help that Samsung grapples with a fundamentally different challenge than Apple. Samsung is forced to lead the space, combat a wave of aggressive Chinese competitors, and constantly prove why it deserves to be the king of Android hardware. It has to innovate in public, iterate openly, and deal with the early design missteps that come with pioneering new categories.

When everyday people see the Z Fold 8 in public or read reviews praising its new wide-body format, they don’t necessarily think about switching to Android. Instead, they think, “If a folding phone can finally look and feel this good, I can’t wait to see what Apple does with an iPhone Fold.” Samsung is doing all the heavy lifting of educating the public and legitimizing the form factor, only for Apple to potentially reap the rewards.

Cards on the table, I do not like iOS, but I’m under no illusions that Apple will have optimized every single aspect of the experience to maximize the experience on the inner and outer screen. Android’s foldable software has improved significantly over the years, but app optimization across varying aspect ratios on Android remains a hit-or-miss affair depending on whether developers care to update their apps. I’m having a great time, but some things could be better. Apple doesn’t have that problem—when Apple drops a new form factor, developers fall in line almost immediately.

We might have differing opinions on our mobile OS of choice, but 9to5Mac’s own Fernando Silva had some very positive things to say about the wider Galaxy Z Fold 8. While we’ve had folding devices for almost a decade, it’s interesting to see the critiques from an Apple-centric position. I implore you to go check it out.

In hindsight, the iPad Mini was the very first step ahead of a potential iPhone Fold. It’s a compact tablet running iPadOS with multi-window capabilities tailored for small-format tablet displays. The second step was the ultra-thin design language introduced with the iPhone Air. Apple’s undoubted prowess in the tablet space has likely held back some internal ambitions to ship a folding phone. They didn’t want to cannibalize their own iPad Mini sales until the market was mature enough to justify merging those two product lines. The tech market is mature now, so for Apple, it’s clearly time to enter the space.

When an iPhone user looks at a Galaxy Z Fold 8, they see an incredible piece of engineering, but they also see One UI, a different app ecosystem, and a departure from their comfort zone. Instead of acting as a gateway to convert those users to Samsung, the Z Fold 8 serves as a proof of concept.

It proves to the “average user” – a phrase I’m not all that fond of – that folding phones are no longer delicate, awkward experiments with annoying aspect ratios. It reassures them that the hardware is ready, leaving them content to simply wait for Apple to drop its own version. Samsung has built a fantastic device that, annoyingly, has accidentally become the ultimate marketing campaign for Apple’s next big thing.

title: Belkin just released four Android Find Hub trackers; one is a full wallet
snippet: More companies are getting on board with trackers that work with the Android Find Hub network, and Belkin is the latest with four different designs. more…
fullText:
More companies are getting on board with trackers that work with the Android Find Hub network, and Belkin is the latest with four different designs.

Trackers come in all shapes and sizes, as long as the size is small and the shape is circular or rectangular. Belkin is mostly sticking to that unwritten rule with several entries in its new SureFind lineup starting at $15.

The smallest and most familiar tracker is the SureFind Spot. It’s the cheapest of the bunch at $15, and it looks a lot like an Apple AirTag, with a keyring included. The SureFind Loop Cable Tag is similar, but the fabric loop doubles as a spare USB-C cable. It’s a little more robust than the Spot, but it fits a similar profile for bags or everyday carry items that don’t require a compact solution. It also charges via USB-C, so it doesn’t need a coin-cell replacement every so often. The SureFind Loop Cable Tag will cost $24.99.

Belkin also released a card-shaped Android Find Hub tracker. Just like other tracker cards, the SureFind Card fits into most wallets and takes up no more space than a credit card. Its ultra-thin profile opens it up to other hiding places, as well. Belkin’s tracker card is IP68 for water and dust-resistance, too. It’s priced in the same area as the Loop Tag, at $26.99.

	

Of all the trackers Belkin announced, the last one is the most unique. We’ve seen the form-factor before, but it’s a welcome one. You could opt to slide a tracking card into your wallet, or you could skip that step and buy a wallet that connects to Google’s Find Hub network (and Apple’s Find My, though not at the same time).

Belkin’s SureFind Wallet Stand shows up in your Find Hub app like every other tracker, but it can’t be easily removed if someone were to take it. It doubles as a magnetic phone stand and comes in a thin compact profile that allows you to store a couple of cards. It’s the most expensive tracker Belkin released at IFA, coming in at $39.99.

Belkin says the SureFind Spot, Loop Cable Tag, and Card will be available starting this month from Amazon and its online store. The SureFind Wallet Stand will go on sale at the beginning of October.

title: Google will not have to sell AdX business, but it will have to make changes
snippet: Following a prior court battle, a judge has now ruled that Google won’t have to sell off its AdX (ad exchange) business after all, and will instead have to make some undisclosed behavioral changes. more…
fullText:
Following a prior court battle, a judge has now ruled that Google won’t have to sell off its AdX (ad exchange) business after all, and will instead have to make some undisclosed behavioral changes.

As reported by Bloomberg and The New York Times, Google will not have to sell off its AdX business. Judge Leonie Brinkema rejected the DOJ’s move to force the sale of that business which would have also make the auction logic behind ad placements public information. 

While Google won’t have to sell off the business or reveal auction logic, the Judge did propose “behavioral changes.”

We’ll know more in 14 days when the decision is unsealed, as both Google and the DOJ will be able to use that time to make any needed redactions. 

	

Still, it’s a major victory on Google’s part. The 2025 ruling still finds Google guilty of breaking the law to protect a monopoly on advertising, but as ArsTechnica points out, the sale of AdX could have made an impact in the rest of Google’s advertising business even if the ad exchange in particular isn’t the biggest part of that business.

fullText:
Apple has three new flagship iPhones launching next week: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and iPhone Ultra. Apple’s Pro models will have several advantages over the Ultra, but here are three ways the high-end Ultra will come out on top.

#1: Larger (and smaller) displays

Dummy models for iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max

5.5-inch cover display

7.8-inch inner display

This compares to iPhone 18 Pro’s 6.3-inch screen and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max.

Essentially, iPhone Ultra provides both a larger display than the Pro models and also a smaller one. As a result, it will be the better choice for anyone wanting the largest iPhone screen. But it could also be a winner for fans of small phones, like the discontinued iPhone mini.

Additionally, the sleek, Air-inspired design of iPhone Ultra should be more comfortable in the hand than Apple’s bulkier Pro models.

iPad mini pictured

Though iPhone Ultra will have a few hardware drawbacks compared to iPhone 18 Pro, it’s likely in the software experience that it will earn its ‘Ultra’ branding.

Side-by-side apps are rumored to be an exclusive multitasking feature of iPhone Ultra. When unfolded, you’ll be able to keep two apps active on-screen at all times. Drag and drop will even be supported between apps.

fullText:
Good morning and happy Thursday. Today I’m watching every minute of M. Night Shyamalan’s new YouTube video on the making of Signs, trying to convince myself I don’t need the Sonos Ace Ultra headphones, and using this helpful guide to finally install a local AI model on my M4 Pro Mac Mini.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column.

⭐️ Starred

Another Android Drop is here, and it comes with some legitimately useful new features. But one feels designed specifically for me and my forgetfulness, and I can’t wait to use it all the time.

	

Gemini has been updated to work with Find Hub, Google’s tool for tracking phones and other gadgets in the ecosystem, to remember the location of physical objects. “Hey Google, remember that I left my spare key inside the hollowed-out copy of Infinite Jest on my bookshelf.” I’m a big fan of these kinds of small, tangible improvements to Android that most people, not just those on the latest version or running a Pixel, will benefit from.

The other new features include a Motion Assist accessibility feature to counteract motion sickness in the car; a Gemini-powered Live Guide accessibility feature that uses AI to “offer descriptions of what’s in front of you”; and a Keep integration inside Google Messages that lets people co-create shopping or packing lists.

Read more: Pixel 11 series getting early September update, not Android 17 QPR1

✉️ Inbox

IFA is here, and that means there are a bunch of gadgets to talk about.

Poco F9 Pro and F9 Ultra launch with 185Hz panels, 8 Elite Gen 5 chips, and huge batteries. Xiaomi’s sub-brand, Poco, used to be known for its lower-priced devices, but now that everything’s expensive, the company is leaning into specs. These feature massive batteries and, on the Ultra, an honest-to-goodness subwoofer that sounds pretty great.

Roku launches its first OLED TVs, available now starting at $999. Roku may be an advertising company at heart, but it still has to make hardware, and its latest TVs are OLEDs that are pretty competitive, and a lot cheaper. They’re also Amazon exclusives for now.

Sony’s new ULT Tower party speakers start at $450. I need to meet the person spending $1500 on a party speaker — because I want to attend that party.

Razer Prio is an Android and iPhone game controller that folds down to roughly the size of a credit card. I have a million portable game controllers, from multiple generations of the Razer Kishi to the Backbone One to basically anything 8BitDo releases. And yet I will still buy this because it looks so darn cute folded up.

Samsung’s latest Galaxy Book 6 starts at $799 with 8GB of RAM. The Korean giant, along with Dell, is announcing a MacBook Neo competitor powered by Intel’s ultra-efficient Wildcat Lake chips.

Govee’s new ceiling light and LED strips are mood boosters with some AI sprinkled in. Govee’s new ceiling light contains “vitality spectrum technology” to keep people more alert during the dark winter months. Will it work? You can pay $399 to find out.

Belkin says its new ‘BoostSolid’ Qi2 batteries last 3x longer than other magnetic power banks. The accessory company is leaning on solid-state battery tech to outlast the competition, which means less e-waste.

Belkin just released four Android Find Hub trackers; one is a full wallet

Philips Hue adds HDMI-free and 4K Sync Box, Nanoleaf partnership, and exciting app upgrades. I’m a big fan of Hue products, so these cheaper options are music to my ears.

Now, onto the news of the day.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is so popular that Samsung is stealing parts from next year’s phones just to make more. A headline that feels perfectly tailored for 2026: Samsung’s unlikely ascension meets a component crisis that’s only getting worse.

Oppo Find X10 reportedly has an 8,000 mAh battery and top-tier specs for a ‘base’ flagship. Oppo has absolutely no chill, and I love it. Can’t wait for this one.

Gemini 3.8 Flash rolling out three weeks after last release. Google is fast-running its Gemini 3.x Flash releases in an effort to make us forget that its newest Pro model is nearly three months late.

MrBeast will try to survive ‘the planet’s most unforgiving landscapes’ using Gemini and Fitbit Air in deal with Google. Google should stick to partnering with the better Jimmy, in my opinion.

Pixel 11 series can now join the Android 17 QPR2 Beta. If you’re a Pixel 11 owner, you can now skip ahead to December’s upcoming Android release and join the blur club.

Google rolling out Pixel Watch 5 September update

Android Auto tests Quick Settings and hilarious ‘Jimothy’ weather Easter egg [Gallery]. Jimothy is a national hero, and I’m so glad he’s getting the respect he deserves.

Android Auto 17.6 update rolling out with redesigned logo [Gallery]

YouTube overhauls its app-to-TV experience, shared Wi-Fi network no longer required. My phone’s most-used app is quickly becoming my TV’s most-used endpoint, and this is going to make it even easier to cast to it.

Google will not have to sell AdX business, but it will have to make changes. Despite Google being found guilty of running an illegal advertising monopoly, a judge is not forcing it to break up its ad business.

Google Home update restores support for older Chromecast streamers, Home Mini. 

WhatsApp for Android loophole lets private photos be accessed without unlocking. Not a huge security issue, but one worth knowing if only to learn what setting to disable to prevent it from happening.

MapQuest is back, at the top of the charts, and rushing to add Android Auto support. Thought it was a one-night stand? Nope, MapQuest is in it for the long haul.

Google’s next Pixel Fold reportedly adopting the same crease-less display as Apple. But more importantly, will the next Pixel Fold revert back to its original passport shape? 

Google Pixel adding ‘Battery usage summaries,’ rolling out on Pixel 10 and newer

🇩🇪 Upcoming

It’s IFA time, which means the tech press and analysts convene in Berlin for bratwurst, bier, and briefings.

While 9to5Google covers a lot of the miscellany, we don’t typically get to the crazier stuff, like this Acer gaming handheld/netbook concept that will almost certainly never be made.

title: An Hour of Gundam: Rogue Orbit Made Me Feverish for More Robot Combat
snippet: The game seems geared more toward melee action than 3D zero-G combat — think less Armored Core and more Dynasty Warriors or Virtual On.
fullText:
When I’m piloting a big robot in a video game, I want it to have a big personality and an even bigger punch. After playing an hour of Gundam: Rogue Orbit, it seems the game will have both. But there’s still a lot to discover about Bandai Namco’s next entry in the giant robot franchise, due out March 5, 2027.

My virtual preview offered two missions and three premade mobile suits (the franchise’s name for the piloted robots) to choose from. The hour was enough to run through both stages with all three mobile suits, each equipped with a different melee weapon. One stage was an enemy gauntlet ending in a miniboss, while the other was a full-fledged boss battle. In the final game, you’ll be able to customize your robot kits, but we didn’t see that functionality because Bandai Namco wanted us focused entirely on the gameplay.

One thing was clear: This isn’t another Armored Core copy. While I loved 2023’s Armored Core 6: Fires of Rubicon, its dizzying array of parts and weapons could be a chore to optimize for the game’s blindingly fast, three-dimensional combat. From what I saw in the preview, Rogue Orbit takes a different, simpler approach. Forget about the Z-axis; just worry about jumping and dashing around, as in most modern melee action games.

True, I had to suspend my disbelief that my mobile suit was hopping around with normal-feeling gravity on the outside of a space station, but I’m betting this trims away a lot of zero-g bother to avoid the awkwardness of floaty jumps. 

Unlike other mech games filled with long-range beam cannons and missiles, Rogue Orbit’s fights seem constrained to melee range only. Whether that was the result of our preview being limited to a trio of mobile suits with swords, lances and whips, or reflects the whole game, I didn’t mind. Ranged combat was limited to support equipment, like a set of orbiting drones that fired when I dashed.

Throughout the preview, I ran across space stations cutting and stabbing through an assortment of enemies, using different skills tuned to my weapons. The sword got a rad slash with trailing explosions, while the whip could be uncoiled for slightly longer-ranged swipes and the lance got a drill-dash to reposition my mobile suit. The combat felt polished, even with half a year to go before the game’s launch, with every attack triggering a momentary pause on contact — a satisfying touch that let me relish the damage I was dishing out and savor my assortment of rad skills.

Ultimately, Rogue Orbit’s combat gameplay felt like Dynasty Warriors or Virtual On (without the twin stick controls), using special skills until my ability gauge ran out and peppering in normal attacks until it charged back up. I had an ultimate attack as well, which, in the preview, gave me unlimited dashes for a limited time until I pulled the ability’s trigger, sending a volley of beams lancing down at my target. In the full game, players will be able to switch between different ultimate attacks.

The short preview was more a tease than a dive into the complexities of the game, and it sure was fun to pummel foes with something that looked like a mobile suit. But the big question I left with was: Does this feel like a Gundam game yet?

The current HUD for the game — from left to right: health, support items, ultimate ability (in the middle), special attack skills and weapon skills.Bandai Namco/Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

How much Gundam is there yet to discover in Rogue Orbit?

Given the brevity of the preview, I didn’t expect to get much context about the characters or plot. Like most latter-day Gundam media, Rogue Orbit is set in a new universe, so don’t expect to see anything from the Federation or Zeon of the original Universal Century setting. Haro, the friendly green, ball-shaped droid from the first Gundam show, does appear in the marketing. (I’m also praying that a masked, Char Aznable-like character will show up, a recurring feature of the franchise.)

From details dropped in the recent trailer and the preview, players will control RE-X, a seemingly human male who was “created” to control a Gundam, the franchise’s special category of humanoid robot mobile suits (his is called Gundam Helix). There are a few other characters in your ship’s crew, including the commander April and the heroine Sophia, who will accompany you. 

The Giant is one of many foes awaiting players in Rogue Orbit.Bandai Namco/Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

Where many Gundam shows and media lean into a political clash between factions of humanity and their armadas of mobile suits, Rogue Orbit seems to be setting up a xenomorphic threat. The enemies I attacked in my preview all seemed organic and monstrous rather than mechanical. While the skulduggery and power clashes result in some of the best conflicts and themes in Gundam, centering Rogue Orbit on a humans-versus-aliens threat (or enemies looking like aliens) opens the door to some intriguing opportunities — by which I mean, huge fantasy-esque bosses that aren’t mechanical Mobile Armors.

At the end of the first mission on the space station exterior, I was clashing with an ogre-like humanoid mini-boss labeled The Giant, who had his own health bar and stagger meter. Similar to other games with those features, once I whittled the latter down enough, the mini-boss went down for a few moments to let me get a few hits in. When I whacked a limb enough, it became disabled, limiting the boss’s attack capabilities.

Players must face the Drake, a large boss with flying attacks, in one mission.Bandai Namco/Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

The second mission was entirely set around confronting a massive alien dragon called the Drake, which took awhile to wear down. In addition to dodging swiping claws and avoiding strings of beams, the Drake has a tail and wings I could hit hard enough to break to temporarily disable some of the meaner blows of the scaly boss. Neither mission was too difficult and I finished both multiple times, but during the preview I only had the three premade kits and no additional difficulty levels to try out. 

From what little I saw, there’s a lot waiting for action-combat fans, though there’s plenty of mechanics, kit customization, story details and encounter complexity left to be revealed about the game. I’m still on the fence for how “Gundam” it may end up feeling in the long run, but the combat’s polish is promising — and enough to have me looking forward to when I can climb into the cockpit again.

Gundam: Rogue Orbit will release on March 5, 2027 for PC, Xbox X/S and PS5.

title: Report: Apple Watch shipments rise 14% in Q2 as overall market drops
snippet: A new Counterpoint Research report shows Apple, Garmin, and Huawei bucking a market-wide decline in smartwatch shipments in Q2 2026, with Huawei reaching a record share of global shipments. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new Counterpoint Research report shows Apple, Garmin, and Huawei bucking a market-wide decline in smartwatch shipments in Q2 2026, with Huawei reaching a record share of global shipments. Here are the details.

Apple records growth across all regions

In a new report published yesterday, Counterpoint Research says the smartwatch market saw a 4% year-over-year decline in global shipments in the second quarter of 2026.

According to the report, Apple saw the biggest jump, with shipments up 14% year over year and accounting for 20.1% of global smartwatch shipments. This kept Apple in second place, behind Huawei, which saw shipments grow 1% year over year and held a 21.8% share.

The ranking continues with Imoo, which held a 7.8% share despite a 3% year-over-year drop in shipments, followed by Xiaomi at 6.1% with a whopping 38% decline. Garmin held a 5.6% share after shipments grew 11%, while other brands collectively accounted for the remaining 38.5%, with shipments down 8% year over year.

Here’s Anshika Jain, Principal Analyst at Counterpoint Research, on Apple’s performance for the quarter, compared with its closest competitors:

“Huawei led the market shipments in Q2 2026, while Apple recorded the fastest YoY growth among the top five brands. Apple recorded growth across all regions, driven by the continued adoption of its refreshed late-2025 lineup. The Apple Watch Series 11 and Watch SE 3 together accounted for over 80% of Apple’s global shipments in Q2 2026. China was the primary driver of Huawei’s growth, accounting for approximately 80% of its global shipments.”

The report also noted that Apple recorded the fastest growth among the top five brands in China for the quarter, “signaling its recovery following the decline seen in the same quarter of 2025,” with the country’s consumer electronics subsidy program also helping boost smartwatch sales.

title: Should You Buy a New iPhone From Apple, a Carrier or Unlocked? Here’s What to Know
snippet: You have a lot of options when buying a new iPhone. In this guide, we walk you through the decision process of exactly where to buy and whether to get an unlocked one.
fullText:
You might be planning to get a new iPhone, be it the rumored iPhone 18 Pro or the highly anticipated foldable iPhone Ultra. But besides choosing which phone to get, the next big question you might be pondering is “Where should I buy my phone?” Should you get it directly from Apple or through a carrier? 

Both methods have their pros and cons, and neither is best for everyone. Perhaps you like the idea of owning your phone outright without going through a third party. Or maybe you’d rather spread out your payments over time. Or perhaps you’re looking to upgrade your phone and switch carriers at the same time. Depending on your answer, you might prefer one path over the other. 

In this guide, we walk you through the process of deciding exactly where to buy your new iPhone, be it directly from Apple or through a wireless provider.

This article was made possible in part by T-Mobile. It was written and edited independently without partner oversight.

Buy directly from Apple

Apple will glady sell you its newest phone and revamped its Upgrade program to let people lease their next iPhone.Jeff Carlson/CNET

Since Apple makes the iPhone, it makes a lot of sense to simply buy the phone directly from the Apple Store. Though buying your iPhone from Apple is a common practice in a lot of countries, it’s not quite as popular here in the US due to the attractive financing options that wireless carriers offer. But buying your phone straight from Apple has its benefits. 

The primary reason to go through Apple is that you can buy the phone without being beholden to a wireless carrier. You have options. Instead of locking yourself down to one wireless carrier for multiple years, buying directly from Apple lets you get the phone completely unlocked.

Apple sells both unlocked iPhones and models tied to a specific carrier. The price is nearly the same, depending on which iPhone you get. But Apple drops the price by $30 when you buy and activate a new iPhone on a carrier at the time of purchase for models like the iPhone 17, which costs $829 unlocked or $799 after a carrier discount.

Unlocked models can be used with nearly any carrier you want, whether it’s a major carrier such as T-Mobile and AT&T or a smaller one such as Mint Mobile or Cricket Mobile. You can also swap out carriers every so often if you feel like it. While your iPhone may cost a pretty penny in the initial purchase, you could save on monthly bills in the long run, depending on your plan. 

Another strong reason to get an unlocked phone is if you travel a lot and want to use international travel eSIMs from companies such as Airalo or Saily. These eSIMs only work on unlocked phones. Otherwise, you’re stuck with your carrier’s international data plans, which are often a lot more expensive. 

If you don’t have the means to purchase the phone outright, you could opt for Apple’s Upgrade program, which lets you lease the phone through Klarna for 12 or 24 months. The phone will still be unlocked, but you’ll have to commit to one of the big three carriers: AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon. 

Buy from a wireless provider

T-Mobile, Verizon and AT&T offer a variety of installment plans and trade-in deals on new iPhones.Joseph Maldonado/CNET

While there is a lot of freedom in buying an iPhone directly from Apple, it comes at a considerable cost. Even the most entry-level iPhone will cost you more than $600 upfront, while more premium handsets can easily cost over $1,000. On top of that, rising component costs could mean even higher prices going forward. It’s no wonder that so many Americans opt for carrier-based financing to purchase their phone. The iPhone 18 Pro could see a price hike, according to a Bloomberg report.

Not all carriers will offer financing, but the big three (AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon) certainly do. In addition to 12- and 24-month installments, some also offer financing up to 36 months, which is more than what Apple’s Upgrade program does. This can really help spread out your payments if you don’t mind sticking with one carrier for an extended period. 

Beyond just being able to pay over time, purchasing an iPhone through your wireless carrier has other benefits, too. Carriers like T-Mobile, for example, offer a 5-year price guarantee on future handsets, which is especially attractive in times of economic uncertainty. 

If you do plan to switch carriers when you buy a new phone, there are potentially even more incentives. Carriers often have new phone deals and could even offer financial assistance to pay off your current phone if you make the switch. There are also some that offer steep discounts if you trade in an existing phone. Sometimes, these incentives come in the form of bill credits, instead of an upfront discount or cashback.

Now that you have an idea about buying a new iPhone, check out our comprehensive guide to switching carriers if you’re looking for more insight on how to navigate the process.

title: Oppo confirms Find X10 Pro Max and its triple 200MP camera setup will launch this month
snippet: As it gears up for launch later this month, Oppo has teased the Find X10 Pro Max with its new addition to the lineup and a triple 200MP camera setup that sounds a bit insane. more…
fullText:
As it gears up for launch later this month, Oppo has teased the Find X10 Pro Max with its new addition to the lineup and a triple 200MP camera setup that sounds a bit insane.

In a post on Weibo, Oppo teases that the Find X10 Pro Max will be the “most powerful” device in its class in regards to imaging this year, and it certainly sounds like it.

As rumored, the post confirms that the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max will come with not one, not two, but three 200MP cameras around back. The main sensor has “DeepPix technology” along with improvements to dynamic range and stabilization, all while managing f/1.5 aperture for increased light capture. The 200MP ultrawide shooter features a 124-degree field-of-view and f/2.2 aperture. The telephoto camera, finally, pairs its 200MP sensor with even better stabilization compared to the main sensor, f/2.1 aperture, and has macro capabilities. The only thing not mentioned is the optical zoom. 

All three cameras can capture in 8K, the post mentions. 

	

It sounds wild, and we’ll find out more soon as the Find X10 series is now confirmed to be launching in September, and more teasers are also set to drop in the coming days, too, the post teases.

title: Pixel 11 lets you make any Camera Look default with this buried setting
snippet: The Pixel 11 series is out in the hands of plenty of (hopefully) happy users, and for the most part, I can count myself among them. This generation marks a massive shift for the camera in particular, as Google has finally loosened up its HDR-centric grip on processing. Really, the only big downsides with Camera Looks appeared to be how it saved your default look — and, as it turns out, there’s a setting to fix that, too. more…
fullText:
The Pixel 11 series is out in the hands of plenty of (hopefully) happy users, and for the most part, I can count myself among them. This generation marks a massive shift for the camera in particular, as Google has finally loosened up its HDR-centric grip on processing. Really, the only big downsides with Camera Looks appeared to be how it saved your default look — and, as it turns out, there’s a setting to fix that, too.

This tip-slash-correction comes via Google’s PR team, which reached out to me last night to let me know that, despite what I found during my hands-on time with Camera Looks, you actually aren’t limited to Google’s four “default” looks as, you know, your default. While Original, Natural, Shadows, and Vanilla are all available under a “Default Look” dropdown menu, if you prefer some of the Pixel 11’s more unique styles — Velvet, Classic, Digi, etc. — those can be saved as your standard preset option.

If you’d rather have complete control over your default, grab your Pixel 11, tap the settings icon in the lower-left corner of the camera app, then tap the triple-dot overflow menu icon in the upper-right. Towards the bottom of the list, look for the Photo menu options, then toggle “Always use selected look” on.

Now, if you return to the Looks menu, selecting any of Google’s non-default options will still be saved as your preference when you leave the app. Whenever one of these more stylized options is selected as your main shooting mode, you’ll see its name briefly appear in the lower-right corner when opening the app, along with a purple Looks icon that sticks around indefinitely. Unlike with one of Google’s four standard processing modes, that permanent Looks icon drops you directly into this menu; you’ll have to hit Back from here to return to other settings like exposure and white balance.

	

It’s honestly great to see that Google does allow Pixel 11 users to save any of these shooting modes  as what’s available immediately upon launching the camera, though I won’t pretend it’s not a bit convoluted to split default preferences into two completely different experiences. But hey, it’s early days for Camera Looks — maybe the Pixel 12 will launch with a more refined UX that unifies this into one slightly-more organized package.

title: Disney+ loses Google Cast support in some countries
snippet: Yet another patent dispute with Disney+ is causing the app to lose Google Cast support in select countries. more…
fullText:
Yet another patent dispute with Disney+ is causing the app to lose Google Cast support in select countries.

Disney has been battling, and losing, in a patent battle with “InterDigital” in recent months. This previously caused the app to lose support for 4K HDR playback in Dolby Vision and 3D content in some regions, which has come and gone in the time since. 

The latest impact is around Google Cast functionality, which is actively being disabled in some regions. BroadcastNow and T3N reported on the dispute, which has led to an injunction against Disney+ in Germany and The Netherlands. While Disney can (and almost certainly will) appeal, the app is currently barred from supporting Cast in these regions.

A notice is already appearing for some users (translated) when trying to cast:

	

Streaming via Chromecast is not available in your country of origin.

title: Apple’s Foldable iPhone Ultra Could Launch Tomorrow, but Arrive Later
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro could be upstaged by Apple’s first foldable this year, though the iPhone Ultra might be hard to get at launch.
fullText:
The iPhone Ultra will use Touch ID rather than Face ID, reportedly because there wasn't enough room in the thin chassis for a TrueDepth camera system.

																			Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET
												
			
				

Key takeaways

The foldable iPhone Ultra’s release date will likely be announced on Sept. 9, but it won’t come out that day.

Current rumors suggest it will hit store shelves later in September, or even October or November.

The first foldable iPhone will likely be a book-style format, potentially followed by a Razr-style clamshell design.

Design leaks suggest a wider, squatter look, similar to the original Google Pixel Fold.

It’s expected to cost between $2,000 and $2,500.

Apple’s fall launch event is Wednesday, and it could mean that Samsung, Google and Motorola may have to share the foldable spotlight with a new rival. After years of rumors, mounting reports suggest this could finally be the year Apple launches its first foldable iPhone, which might be called the iPhone Ultra.

But there could be a wait between announcing the foldable and getting it into people’s hands. Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, as reported by MacRumors, says Apple could unveil the foldable alongside the iPhone 18 lineup, but the company may wait until later in the year to put it on sale, similar to the iPhone X launch in 2017. Apple sent out invites to an event on Sept. 9, where we expect the next iPhones to be unveiled — and likely the foldable as well.

That event will be a landmark for other reasons beyond the potential launch of a folding iPhone. It’s the first since outgoing CEO Tim Cook formally handed the keys to the Apple kingdom to its new head, John Ternus. To celebrate this occasion, CNET has been reliving fun and pivotal moments from our decades covering the company with our Apple a Day series.

A folding iPhone is expected to arrive at a starting price north of $2,000, with Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reporting that Apple has discussed starting prices as high as $2,200 — with larger storage configurations nearing $3,000. The name that’s stuck in the rumor mill for years, the iPhone Fold, might even change before it hits store shelves. Leaks increasingly point to “iPhone Ultra,” a label that would elevate the device above the Pro lineup and signal a new tier of Apple hardware.

Mock-ups of potential iPhone foldables, including a clamshell “iPhone Flip” on the left and a book-style foldable on the right, along with a flat iPhone for comparison on the bottom.

Zain bin Awais/CNET

While the inside of the iPhone foldable will have a near tablet-sized 7.8-inch display, it may not have all the functionality of an iPad, Gurman recently told Yahoo Tech. From what he’s heard, the Mac-like multitasking that Apple added to iPadOS won’t quite be what’s in the foldable iPhone. Instead, expect side-by-side app layouts that should still let users drag and drop things between them.

We’ve gotten far more design leaks suggesting how Apple’s foldable may look. Most suggest that the iPhone Fold will be a book-style foldable that’s squat and wide, looking more like the original Pixel Fold or the new Galaxy Fold 8 than taller, thinner models, such as the Galaxy Z Fold 7 or the Pixel 10 Pro Fold.

The screen on the iPhone Fold is rumored to have little or no crease, according to a recent report by the Chinese publication UDN. Screen creases, especially on early foldable phones, have long annoyed consumers and critics, and they still remain, despite the seam getting less noticeable over the years. Even Samsung’s most advanced Galaxy Z TriFold has two screen creases, one for each of its hinges. It would be a major breakthrough if Apple were to find a way to fold a screen in half without leaving a crease.

Another report from leaker Fixed Focus Digital on Weibo suggests that Apple’s hinges could be made of liquid metal, an alloy possibly provided by Liquidmetal Technologies, with which Apple has had an exclusive contract since 2010. It’s been the topic of many rumors since then and the basis of several patent applications, but so far, no products other than the SIM ejector tool that once shipped with iPhone models.

Even days before its potential release, we’ve yet to hear any official word on a foldable iPhone from Apple.

	

			

Foldable phones represent a tiny fraction of all phones sold globally. In a recent survey, CNET found that 64% of people said they don’t want a foldable phone. But those numbers could change if Apple were to sell a foldable iPhone. As of April, IDC analysts predict that global foldable sales will jump 19% if the iPhone Fold launches in 2026, with Apple’s folding device capturing around 24% of the global market share.

A lot of hope and high expectations have been placed on Apple’s release of a foldable phone. And if rumors are correct, we won’t have to wait much longer for the company to do so.

iPhone Fold release date: It could launch on Sept. 9… or in 2027

Apple’s invite to its Sept. 9 event has the tagline “Surprise and shine.”Apple

Apple has neither confirmed the iPhone Fold nor announced a release date. But analysts and rumors have predicted that the foldable could come out in 2026 or be pushed until next year. So while the upcoming Sept. 9 Apple event is the most likely release date, as the first device of its kind released by Apple, we can’t be sure until the company shows it off. 

As for timing, since the iPhone Air was released alongside the iPhone 17 models, the Fold is likely to come alongside the iPhone 18 series, which is expected to launch during the Sept. 9 event. Apple could even delay the launch of the standard iPhone 18 to the spring of 2027 to make room for the iPhone Fold in Apple’s Sept. 9 launch, according to an ET News report. Given that Samsung offsets its standard and foldable phone releases at Unpacked events months apart from each other, Apple could do the same.

Once the foldable iPhone does go on sale, it may be hard to get. Leaker Fixed Focus Digital said in a Weibo post that although the initial run of foldable iPhones will be around 10 million units, production could take three to five months to ramp up. That’s about 30% to 40% slower than the iPhone 17’s production of 5 million units per month. That could mean a supply shortage delaying people from picking up the folding iPhone for some time after its launch.

It’s been an open secret for years that Apple is working toward a foldable iPhone, but buzz and possible release dates have been floated for just as long. Early rumors pointed to 2021 as a potential target date, but the year passed with no foldable iPhone in sight, as have successive rumors for potential releases in 2023 and 2025. 

Read more: Top Foldable Phones for 2026

	

			

iPhone Fold price

Kuo, the analyst, predicted that a book-style iPhone foldable coming in 2026 could be priced anywhere from $2,000 to $2,500, as it’s “expected to generate strong replacement demand — despite the premium price — provided quality meets expectations.”

The day before Apple is expected to reveal the foldable iPhone, Bloomberg’s Gurman reported that the company had still been discussing the price as recently as weeks before the event. It could start as high as $2,200, with higher storage configurations pushing the price north of $3,000.

A report last year found that half of American consumers are interested in buying a foldable phone, though Apple customers are slightly less willing to make the leap than Samsung or LG users. Perhaps the “Apple effect” will change those stats if and when a foldable iPhone ever becomes a reality.

Although Motorola offers one of the most affordable folding phones with its clamshell Razr at $800, most others in the category are book-style foldables, such as the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Pixel 10 Pro Fold, which cost around twice as much as most flagship phones. We don’t expect a foldable iPhone to be cheaper than its rivals, which start around $2,000.

iPhone Fold specs

There are no confirmed specs for the iPhone Fold; Apple hasn’t even confirmed one exists or is coming out. Even if we expect it to come out soon, it’s tough to predict what kind of internal specs the iPhone Fold will have. Presumably, Apple will equip it with its most powerful A-series chip, along with enough RAM to handle two or three displays (depending on whether it folds inward or outward and needs a dedicated outer screen). That could mean an A20 Pro chip, if Apple follows precedent in equipping this year’s iPhone Pro models with successors to last year’s A19 Pro silicon.

We do have some predictions for other specs, though only for the rumored book-style Fold (not the clamshell). In March 2024, Kuo predicted the larger Fold could have a 5.5-inch outer screen and a 7.8-inch inner display. When folded, it’s rumored to be 9 millimeters to 9.5mm thick and 4.5mm to 4.8mm when unfolded. Plus, a front-facing camera is also rumored to work whether the phone is folded or unfolded; the phone is also rumored to have two rear cameras.

Kuo predicted that the device would use the same high-density battery cells as used in what he referred to then as the “ultrathin iPhone 17,” which presumably meant the iPhone Air. But that trim thickness means the foldable may forgo Face ID, so the device could end up using Touch ID in a side button. 

Some rumors about hardware have emerged, too. In January, an analyst note seen by MacRumors suggested Apple’s foldable could launch with 12GB of RAM, the same amount in the Galaxy Z Fold 7‘s starting configuration. That could mean Apple doesn’t need much memory to handle multiple screens or isn’t banking on large AI features that require significant RAM.

And we finally have a prediction on the iPhone Fold’s battery, with Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital posting that it could have a 5,500-mAh capacity, as 9to5Mac first reported. That’s larger than batteries on some other foldables. (The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, for example, has a 5,000-mAh battery, but Samsung has been in the foldable game for years and has likely improved efficiency in an effort to slim down its devices.) Yet if the Weibo leak is true, this will be the largest battery ever on an Apple handset. The iPhone 17 Pro Max has a 5,088-mAh battery.

	

			

Design: What will the foldable iPhone look like?

This illustration, according to Apple’s patent filing, shows a “device that bends along a flexible portion, such as a flexible seam associated with a hinge.”

Apple/US Patent and Trademark Office

Apple seems to have taken out every patent under the sun when it comes to foldable displays, including an origami-style folding display, a flip-up display and even a wraparound display. As far back as 2021, a Bloomberg report indicated Apple already had a prototype of a foldable iPhone display, and rumors since then have bounced back and forth between suggesting Apple will opt for either a clamshell- or book-style foldable first. 

In March 2025, Kuo made several specific predictions for Apple’s foldable: It would be a book-style device with a 5.5-inch outer screen that unfolds into a 7.8-inch internal display, measuring 4.5 to 4.8mm thick when unfolded and 9 to 9.5mm when folded. It would also use the same high-density battery cells as the “ultrathin iPhone 17” and include a hinge made of stainless steel and titanium alloy — a favorite material in Apple’s iPhone 16 Pro and Pro Max, as well as the Apple Watch Ultra 3.

A mock-up of the iPhone Fold based on unofficial leaked CAD renders from @SonyDIckson on X. 

Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Per Kuo’s predictions, the foldable will have two rear cameras and a front-facing camera on both the external and internal displays. Most interestingly, he also expects that Apple’s book-style foldable will see the return of Touch ID as a side button, as Face ID might be left out due to space constraints — presumably for the array of depth-of-field sensors and cameras needed for the tech. 

Then there are the renders, which have gone from a trickle to a steady stream through 2026. One set of 3D CAD renders from leaker Sonny Dickson (pictured above) points to a squat, wide design that looks much more like the original Pixel Fold than the tall, thin Galaxy Z Fold 7 or the Honor Magic V6 Foldable. 

iPhone 2026 lineup

CNET’s Jeffrey Hazelwood created these custom renders of what an iPhone 18 Pro might look like.

Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

There’s no guarantee about which phones Apple will release during its usual September window, but the safest bet is on another series of flat phones, which we expect to be the iPhone 18 line. But what else could be coming alongside the usual lineup?

There could be an iPhone Air 2, though rumors conflict over whether to expect one next year. There’s been a lot more evidence of an iPhone Fold, though whether it comes out in 2026 or later remains uncertain. If the iPhone Fold does launch next year, more rumors suggest a clamshell device has been prioritized and may come first. Given reports of Apple researching a book-style foldable, we could get one of those as well. 

In mid-January, MacRumors reportedly saw a research note from analyst Jeff Pu suggesting that the iPhone Fold will pack 12GB of memory — as will the entire iPhone 18 line. Apple never discloses how much RAM its phones include, but spec sites such as GSMArena have reported that the standard iPhone 17 has 8GB of RAM, while the rest of the series (iPhone Air, 17 Pro and Pro Max) all have 12GB. If correct, that means Apple doesn’t think its foldable will need more memory than its standard flat phones; it would have more screen area but potentially no more advanced hardware than its iPhone 18 siblings.

It’s also interesting to see the standard iPhone 18 packing 12GB of memory, as the RAM shortage is predicted to hike prices on phones released in 2026 and potentially even wipe out the cheapest budget phones from the market until memory prices drop enough to make low-cost phones profitable again. Apple may be willing to absorb the costs of a more capable basic iPhone 18 model, or perhaps it’ll pass those costs on to consumers with a price hike. 

	

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Lumb
						

						

							Managing Editor, Mobile						
					

											

								

											David Lumb is a managing editor for the mobile team, covering mobile and gaming spaces. Before CNET, he covered tech, gaming, and culture for TechRadar, Engadget, Popular Mechanics, NBC Asian America, Increment, Fast Company and others. title: Sony WH-1000XM4C launch for $299 alongside two more affordable headphones
snippet: As rumored, Sony is reviving its WH-1000XM4 headphones with a new WH-1000XM4C reboot, bringing some new colors to a much more affordable entry to the market compared to the company’s flagship. more…
fullText:
As rumored, Sony is reviving its WH-1000XM4 headphones with a new WH-1000XM4C reboot, bringing some new colors to a much more affordable entry to the market compared to the company’s flagship.

Sony’s flagship headphones are very good, but they’re also pricey. The current WH-1000XM6 retails for $460, though you can often save when buying on deals. But, now, Sony has a more affordable entry in this lineup with the new WH-1000XM4C.

This is a reboot of Sony’s 2020 flagship, which was equipped with USB-C and all of the sound and ANC you’d expect from a high-end pair of over-ear headphones. 

What’s new? Not a whole lot. Sony says to expect the same overall ANC and audio performance, but with the “latest sound tuning.” The hardware is mostly identical, though with new colors including Lavender, Black, and Platinum Silver.

	

They’re available for $299, well below Sony’s current flagship and in line with competitors such as Nothing Headphone (1). It’s borderline impossible to get a brand new pair of WH-1000XM4 nowadays, and even on the used market, you’re still spending around $250 or so in some cases. You might be able to find WH-1000XM5 for less – Amazon has frequent sales – but it’s likely these will see discounts in time too.

fullText:
Apple TV just wrapped up the third season of its hit sci-fi series Silo, with a fourth and final season already dated for summer next year.

But it seems the streamer has more ambitious plans yet. According to reliable Apple TV reporter Sigmund Judge, Apple is working on a spin-off show that could go into pre-production later in the year.

Apparently, the spinoff will be based on an upcoming Hugh Howey novel, centered on the happenings in Silo 40.

While Apple has not confirmed the plans, and although Howey is publicly denying it, there is one little detail that makes this seem very plausible: the Silo sets have not yet been deconstructed. 

Typically, a show with no planned future (either ended or cancelled) will quickly tear down and sell off sets in order to make room for something else on the production lots. However, Judge reports that filming on Silo season four ended in March, almost six months ago, and yet the sets remain standing. 

This is very good evidence that Apple plans to re-use them in the future, probably for the spin-off reportedly currently in development. 

We have already seen Apple invest heavily in its science fiction franchises with spin-off series like Star City (from the world of For All Mankind) and an announced upcoming series set in the Monarch universe. 

And Silo has clearly been a big viewership hit for the streamer, so it makes sense to keep the content coming.
